# /lore/code-snippets

Source: .brain/resources/lore/code-snippets.svx
SHA-256: 8bd8fa67c8079914a6c27052ff8c7ccea3887ec21139979ff172f080875667a3

# Code snippets quote a pinned source

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

**Design brief; shipped at `a646f7ffd00273d85fbe1d905d9cdb194fdc0f60`.**

`@rat-stack/code-snippets` gives an excerpt its exact source, checks its metadata, and builds both reader views from one model.
See [Write a wiki page](/skills/write-a-wiki-page) for authoring steps and exact repair messages.

Lore explains design choices. [Systems](/systems) documents shipped behavior, as set out in the [project vision](https://github.com/joelhooks/rat-stack/blob/main/VISION.md).

## The problem

A copied excerpt can stop matching its source.
A reader needs the exact revision, file, and selected lines.
An author needs errors that explain how to repair a broken reference.

The package reads [pinned sources](/lore/pinned-sources-can-report-drift) during content generation.
It produces [one snippet model for both renderers](/lore/one-snippet-model-two-renderers).
It reports changed selected lines as warnings without replacing the pinned text.

## The authoring syntax

A Markdown code fence is a block delimited by backticks. It differs from rat-stack's enforcement fence.

Code fences are the only authoring syntax. Authors do not write `<Code>` elements.
The internal component renderer remains an implementation detail.

Fence metadata means options on the opening line of a Markdown code block.
It has these parts:

- An optional language token.
- Whitespace-separated `key=value` pairs.
- At most one highlight set, such as `{3,5-7}`.
- Unquoted or double-quoted values.

The accepted keys are `repo`, `path`, `at`, `lines`, `title`, and `nocheck`.
Unknown keys, duplicate keys, and malformed metadata are errors.

Every published TypeScript fence without `path` must typecheck.
The content build writes each one to `apps/site/dist/doc-fences` as its own module.
`pnpm check` typechecks that directory with `apps/site/tsconfig.doc-fences.json`.
A fragment that cannot compile takes `nocheck="<reason>"`.
`.brain/data/doc-fence-baseline.json` records the opt-out count, and the count only shrinks.

The shipped request records content, selection, and source repository, commit, file, and line numbers:

packages/code-snippets/src/model.ts at c936b94c957ada7199df3ab7b39a330d6e1c644f; lines 17-34; highlighted 23,29. Title: Decoded CodeRequest.

```typescript
export class CodeRequest extends Schema.Class<
  CodeRequest,
  { readonly brand: unique symbol }
>("CodeRequest")({
  body: Schema.String,
  commit: Schema.String,
  configured: Schema.Boolean,
  highlights: Schema.Array(RangeSchema),
  language: Schema.String,
  line: Schema.Int,
  path: Schema.String,
  rangeText: Schema.String,
  ranges: Schema.Array(RangeSchema),
  reference: Schema.Boolean,
  repo: Schema.String,
  sourcePath: Schema.String,
  title: Schema.String,
}) {}
```

`configured` distinguishes metadata fences from ordinary fences. `ranges` carries decoded selections.

A source reference has an empty body. These selected lines enforce the pin and path rules:

packages/code-snippets/src/scanner.ts at a646f7ffd00273d85fbe1d905d9cdb194fdc0f60; lines 180-190,192-197; highlighted 189,193-197. Title: Pinned revision and relative path.

```typescript
const validCommit = (value: string) => {
  for (let index = 0; index < value.length; index += 1) {
    const char = value.charAt(index);

    if (!(char >= "0" && char <= "9") && !(char >= "a" && char <= "f")) {
      return false;
    }
  }

  return value.length === 40;
};
const validPath = (value: string) =>
  !value.startsWith("/") &&
  !value.includes(":") &&
  !value
    .split("/")
    .some((part) => part === ".." || part === "" || part === ".");
```

Paths reject traversal, empty segments, dots, and colons.

For a source reference:

- `repo` identifies a configured repository. It defaults to `rat-stack`.
- `path` names a relative file path.
- `at` pins a full 40-character lowercase commit SHA, never a branch or tag.
- `lines` selects positive, ordered, non-overlapping inclusive ranges.
- Highlights use original source line numbers and stay inside visible ranges.
- Configured fences show at most 25 source lines. Collapsed gaps do not count.

The cap also covers inline fences with metadata. Ordinary fences without metadata keep their renderer and are not capped by this rule.

A `path` reference with body text fails with `CodeBodyWithReference`.

An explicit language wins. An unknown explicit language is an error.
Without a language, a source reference infers it from the file extension.

An unmapped extension or an unlabelled inline fence uses `markdown`.
The adapter maps `svx` to Markdown and `txt` to text; it accepts `javascript` explicitly.

[Schema decoding](/lore/schemas-define-the-boundary) parses unknown metadata into a `CodeRequest` at the boundary.
Later stages receive decoded values.

## The pipeline

Preflight checks every independent snippet job before any generated output is written.

Diagram: Collect produces CodeRequest; resolve produces ResolvedCode; highlight produces HighlightedFile; decorate produces CodeSnippet; preflight permits HTML and agent Markdown emission.

```text
fence nodes
    │ collect and decode
    ▼
CodeRequest
    │ resolve pinned Git object
    ▼
ResolvedCode
    │ tokenize the whole file
    ▼
HighlightedFile
    │ select lines, highlights, and gaps
    ▼
CodeSnippet
    │ all jobs pass preflight
    ├──────────────────────┐
    ▼                      ▼
HTML                   agent Markdown
```

Each stage adds facts. Both renderers use the same final model.

- **Collect**: Walk Markdown syntax-tree code nodes; scan metadata; Schema-decode requests and source locations.
- **Resolve**: Read source text; determine file length and language; check ranges; derive a source link.
- **Highlight**: Produce tokens for every source line.
- **Decorate**: Select numbered lines; attach highlights, collapsed gaps, source details, and diagnostics.
- **Emit**: Write assets only after every independent job passes preflight.

[Whole-file tokenization](/lore/tokenize-before-slicing) comes before range selection.
This preserves the preceding source context for multiline comments and strings.

## Ports and adapters

A port is an application-owned interface. An adapter implements that interface for a provider.
The package follows [ports and adapters](/lore/hexagonal-architecture).

Its core owns stage schemas, errors, and selection rules. Core imports neither Git nor Shiki.

`SourceRepository` resolves repository id, commit, and path through a decoded registry.
Each entry contains `id`, `adapter`, and `location`. Optional fields are `linkTemplate` and the bootstrap `remote`.

The `/git` adapter reads any configured local Git repository.
Mischief configures `rat-stack` to the clone used for generation.
Link templates substitute `{sha}`, `{path}`, `{start}`, and `{end}`.
A GitHub, GitLab, Forgejo, or link-free entry needs no core change.

The [highlighter port](/lore/engine-neutral-tokens-keep-adapters-replaceable) exposes:

- Per-line tokens containing `text`, `role`, and `fontStyle`.
- Language, alias, and theme catalogues.
- An engine fingerprint: an identifier for the highlighter, version, and settings used in cache keys.

The `/shiki` adapter uses the build-only Shiki 4.6.0 pin.
Shiki token types stay inside that adapter.
A `/plain` adapter supplies uncoloured tokens for core tests.

A service is a named interface. A Layer describes how to build a service and supply its dependencies.
A Scope owns resource cleanup.

[Layers](/lore/layer-constructor-pattern) provide the adapters. Shiki acquisition and disposal stay inside a scoped Layer.

Mischief collects Markdown syntax-tree nodes, chooses component renderers, and owns markup, CSS, and reporting.
Syntax styles obey [the fence](/lore/the-fence), including the existing accent rule.

### Cache boundaries

During one build, caches reuse successful results whose inputs cannot change:

- Blob cache: repository, commit, and path.
- Whole-file token cache: content key and engine settings.
- Render cache: the canonical snippet content key.

Snippet decoration also depends on ranges and highlights.
HEAD, diagnostics, and failures do not enter the immutable cache.
There is no persistent cache initially. Content-addressed output and Turbo provide reuse between builds.

## Errors as interface

[Errors are part of the interface](/lore/errors-are-part-of-the-interface).
Each typed error keeps the source location, request context, and a repair instruction.
Range errors include requested ranges and actual file length when available.
Invalid metadata retains raw values because no decoded request exists.

- **Metadata**:
  - Shipped tags: `CodeInvalidProps`, `CodeUnknownKey`, `CodeDuplicateKey`, `CodeMalformedMeta`, `CodeBodyWithReference`
  - Repair: Correct the fence metadata or remove reference body text.
- **Registry**:
  - Shipped tags: `CodeUnknownRepo`, `CodeRepositoryConfigInvalid`
  - Repair: Select a registered id or repair the registry.
- **Source**:
  - Shipped tags: `CodeMissingCommit`, `CodeMissingPath`, `CodeSourceUnavailable`
  - Repair: Correct the pin or path; fetch missing shallow history before generation.
- **Selection**:
  - Shipped tags: `CodeInvalidRanges`, `CodeRangeOutOfBounds`, `CodeHighlightOutsideRanges`, `CodeLineCapExceeded`
  - Repair: Use ordered, visible ranges within file bounds and the line cap.
- **Engine**:
  - Shipped tags: `UnknownLanguage`, `CodeHighlightFailed`
  - Repair: Select a supported language or repair the highlighter adapter.

The report-level `CodeBuildFailed` holds collected failures.
[Error accumulation](/lore/accumulate-independent-errors) uses [`Effect.validate`](https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/blob/effect%404.0.0/packages/effect/src/Effect.ts#L594-L651). `validateAll` is not the operation used here.

A dependent stage stops on failure. Unrelated jobs still run.
No asset writer runs before successful preflight.

[Source drift](/lore/pinned-sources-can-report-drift) produces diagnostics while allowing the build to continue.
The [error model](/lore/error-model) separates expected failures from defects.

## The testing approach

The package ships property tests for these rules. Mischief also tests the renderer integration.

Use a small plain-array reference model for visible line numbers, gaps, and highlights.
Do not copy production selection logic into the model.
See [model-based testing](/lore/model-based-testing) and [tests that earn their place](/lore/tests-that-earn-their-place).

- **P1**: Printing then parsing valid metadata preserves the request.
- **P2**: Every arbitrary metadata string produces a request or a typed failure; parsing never crashes.
- **P3**: Accepted ranges are positive, ordered, disjoint, and strictly within source bounds.
- **P4**: Visible line numbers, collapsed gaps, and highlights match the independent array model.
- **P5**: Selected tokens match whole-file Shiki tokens, including multiline comments and template strings.
- **P6**: HTML, agent Markdown, and pinned source agree on selected text, repository, commit, file, and line numbers.
- **P7**: Exactly `k` independent failures produce `k` diagnostics and no asset writes.
- **P8**: Repeated rendering with an identical content key produces identical bytes. Every output-affecting input participates in the key.

A changed key need not change output bytes. An engine version change can preserve token output.

Use [property-based testing and shrinking](/lore/property-based-testing).
Effect 4 exposes [`Arbitrary.schema`](https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/blob/effect%404.0.0/packages/effect/src/Arbitrary.ts) through `effect/Arbitrary`.
[`it.prop` and `it.effect.prop`](https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/blob/effect%404.0.0/packages/vitest/src/index.ts#L53-L165) accept Schema or Arbitrary inputs.

The package uses 40 runs per property.
P5 exercises Shiki. Other core properties use the plain adapter.

The test suite also checks:

- One exact-message example per error tag at the interface that reports errors.
- Byte comparisons for ordinary fences under the decided default language rule.
- A planted range or slicing bug that makes its property fail.
- Startup bundle checks for the build-only boundary.

Use [tests that earn their place](/lore/tests-that-earn-their-place) for planted-bug checks.
[Agents explore, tests remember](/lore/agents-explore-tests-remember) connects exploration with repeatable behavior checks.

## Prior art and where we differ

- **[rehype-pretty-code](https://rehype-pretty.pages.dev/)**:
  - Reused idea: Fence titles and `{1-3,4}` line highlights.
  - Shipped difference: Add repository, commit, path, and selection keys.
- **[Expressive Code text markers](https://expressive-code.com/key-features/text-markers/)**:
  - Reused idea: Line sets in fence metadata.
  - Shipped difference: Reject malformed or unsupported metadata instead of accepting a broad marker language.
- **[Expressive Code MetaOptions](https://github.com/expressive-code/expressive-code/blob/main/packages/%40expressive-code/core/src/helpers/meta-options.ts)**:
  - Reused idea: A dedicated metadata parser.
  - Shipped difference: Use an allowlist and reject duplicate keys. Its accessors can return the last matching value.
- **[Docusaurus Theme GitHub Codeblock](https://github.com/saucelabs/docusaurus-theme-github-codeblock)**:
  - Reused idea: Import excerpts from GitHub reference URLs.
  - Shipped difference: Resolve local Git objects instead of downloading code.
- **[remark-github-code-import](https://github.com/haocheng6/remark-github-code-import/blob/main/src/utils.ts)**:
  - Reused idea: Import excerpts from GitHub URLs, including commit permalinks.
  - Shipped difference: Keep generation offline; use a configured repository registry.

The scanner accepts only the grammar documented above, a stricter subset than the general `MetaOptions` parser.

## Build-only limits

There is no remote source adapter, mirror synchronization, or persistent snippet cache in this design.
A shallow clone must already contain the pinned commit and file-content Git object.
Generation performs no checkout and no network fetch.

Run `pnpm sources:fetch` explicitly before generation when pinned objects are missing. It uses the configured bootstrap remote and verifies the requested commits.

[Build-time work stays out of requests](/lore/build-time-work-stays-out-of-requests).
The Worker receives static assets. Git access, Shiki, and the snippet package stay in the build.

There is no state machine yet.
This is one scoped Effect over immutable local objects.
It has no retry policy, resumable acquisition, or externally driven state transitions.
A machine would repeat the stage call graph without owning a lifecycle.

[Lifecycles are machines](/lore/lifecycles-are-machines) applies when remote acquisition adds retries, cancellation, or resumability.
That future adapter must use declared Effect actors rather than inline side effects.

See [the glossary](/glossary) for fence metadata and the linked concepts.

# /lore/concurrent-work-needs-an-owner

Source: .brain/resources/lore/concurrent-work-needs-an-owner.svx
SHA-256: 86fda0c7a377d7cf00e3b0e41a5e5e583c2191bc2ba83ba59ad4fb1167d6c809

# Concurrent work needs an owner and a bound

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Choose how many operations may run at once. Give child work an owner that can stop it.
A completed caller must not silently leave its work running.

## Bound collection processing before running it

A traversal processes each input in a collection. An Effect describes work before execution.

`Effect.forEach` describes one Effect per input and collects results in input order.
Its concurrency option bounds active operations.
The input collection can be larger than that bound.
The checked fixture measures active work with a Ref, an Effect value that stores mutable state.

packages/capability/test/fixtures/wiki/bounded-traversal.ts at 4019cffbcbdb282d6f006854ff5b1f26d3b407e0; lines 8-30; highlighted none.

```typescript
    const activity = yield* Ref.make({ active: 0, maximum: 0 });
    const input = Array.from({ length: options.count }, (_, index) => index);

    const results = yield* Effect.forEach(
      input,
      (index) =>
        Effect.acquireUseRelease(
          Ref.update(activity, (state) => ({
            active: state.active + 1,
            maximum: Math.max(state.maximum, state.active + 1),
          })),
          () => Effect.yieldNow.pipe(Effect.andThen(Effect.succeed(index))),
          () =>
            Ref.update(activity, (state) => ({
              ...state,
              active: state.active - 1,
            }))
        ),
      { concurrency: options.concurrency }
    );

    return { ...(yield* Ref.get(activity)), results };
  }
```

The generated test varies both the input count and the bound.
It requires completed work, no remaining activity, input-order results, and a peak that does not exceed the supplied bound.

packages/capability/test/concurrency-ownership.test.ts at 4019cffbcbdb282d6f006854ff5b1f26d3b407e0; lines 7-26; highlighted none.

```typescript
const Traversal = Schema.Struct({
  concurrency: Schema.Literals([1, 2, 3, 4]),
  count: Schema.Literals([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]),
});

it.effect.prop(
  "traversal never exceeds its supplied bound and preserves input order",
  { scenario: Arbitrary.schema(Traversal) },
  ({ scenario }) =>
    Effect.gen(function* traversalBound() {
      const observed = yield* boundedTraversal(scenario);
      expect(observed.maximum).toBeGreaterThan(0);
      expect(observed.maximum).toBeLessThanOrEqual(scenario.concurrency);
      expect(observed.active).toBe(0);
      expect(observed.results).toEqual(
        Array.from({ length: scenario.count }, (_, index) => index)
      );
    })
);

```

The expectation uses the supplied bound. It is independent of the traversal's scheduling algorithm.

A planted violation replaced the bound with `unbounded`.
The property failed with seven active operations against a bound of one. The restored implementation passes.
Measure production limits separately from these generated test counts.

## Stop child work with its Scope

The sandbox writes queued input to a child process through a scoped fiber: child work that stops when its owning Scope closes.
A fiber is an independently running Effect. A Scope owns cleanup.

packages/capability/src/sandbox-subprocess.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 237-242; highlighted none.

```typescript
      const outbox = yield* Queue.unbounded<Uint8Array, Cause.Done>();
      yield* Stream.fromQueue(outbox).pipe(
        Stream.run(handle.stdin),
        Effect.ignore,
        Effect.forkScoped
      );
```

The checked ownership test starts a child that waits indefinitely.
When the owner closes, the child must observe interruption before the enclosing Effect returns.

packages/capability/test/concurrency-ownership.test.ts at 4019cffbcbdb282d6f006854ff5b1f26d3b407e0; lines 30-46; highlighted none.

```typescript
    Effect.gen(function* childOwnership() {
      const started = yield* Deferred.make<boolean>();
      const interrupted = yield* Ref.make(0);
      yield* Effect.scoped(
        Effect.gen(function* ownChild() {
          yield* Deferred.succeed(started, true).pipe(
            Effect.andThen(Effect.never),
            Effect.onInterrupt(() =>
              Ref.update(interrupted, (count) => count + 1)
            ),
            Effect.forkScoped
          );
          yield* Deferred.await(started);
        })
      );
      expect(yield* Ref.get(interrupted)).toBe(1);
    })
```

A Deferred is an Effect value completed once to signal that work started. The test does not depend on an arbitrary sleep.

Use [scopes](/lore/scopes-own-resources) to decide the lifetime before choosing a fork operation.
Different fork operations carry different ownership rules; do not treat their names as interchangeable.

## Consume a stream without promising a bounded queue

The sandbox decodes stdout, splits it into lines, and interprets each protocol message with an Effect.
Its consumer stops after the first completed outcome.

packages/capability/src/sandbox-subprocess.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 254-267,289-298; highlighted none.

```typescript
      const outcome = yield* Stream.decodeText(handle.stdout).pipe(
        Stream.splitLines,
        Stream.filter((line) => line.trim() !== ""),
        Stream.mapEffect(
          (line) =>
            decodeChildMessage(line).pipe(
              Effect.mapError(
                (error) =>
                  new SandboxError({
                    logs: [],
                    message: `Unreadable sandbox message: ${error.message}`,
                    reason: "protocol",
                  })
              ),
            ),
          { concurrency: 8 }
        ),
        Stream.filter(Option.isSome),
        Stream.map((option) => option.value),
        Stream.runHead,
        Effect.mapError((error) =>
          isSandboxError(error)
            ? error
            : new SandboxError({
```

`Stream.mapEffect` keeps decoding and dispatch in the stream description. The consumer does not launch eager Promises for each line.

Backpressure lets the consumer limit how quickly the producer can continue.
An unbounded queue can let the producer keep adding data.

The producer uses `Queue.unbounded`. This code does not prove a bounded producer queue or bounded total memory.
A bounded consumer is not enough when producers can accumulate data faster than it is consumed.

For a growing input, choose a stream and inspect each buffer's policy.
For a known finite collection, a bounded traversal can be enough.
Measure the service's limits before selecting an operational bound.

## Common mistakes

- Create eager Promises before building the owned Effect traversal.
- Detach work that should stop with the caller.
- Bound worker concurrency and claim every upstream buffer is bounded too.
- Copy test counts into production without measuring the provider and host.

## Effect idiom and house rule

- Fibers, traversal bounds and streams compose owned work without replacing the typed Effect description.
- In rat-stack, measure operational limits instead of inventing caps.
- In rat-stack, [machines own finite domain retries and cancellation](/lore/lifecycles-are-machines). Effect's native fibers and schedules still exist.

Next, [validate HTTP responses](/lore/http-responses-need-validation) before treating concurrent provider work as successful.

For work that must survive a crash, read [every task needs an owner](/lore/every-task-needs-an-owner) and the [durability index](/lore/durability).

Return to the [Effect reading order](/lore/effect-basics#read-next).

# /lore/configuration-is-a-dependency

Source: .brain/resources/lore/configuration-is-a-dependency.svx
SHA-256: ed7d7cadaa797b21be7805a46cd53038d4fcd30a702cfb13bb167fde73231f8a

# Configuration is a supplied, validated dependency

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

A service is a named interface. A Layer describes how to build it and supply its dependencies.
Schema defines accepted values and checks data at runtime.

Read configuration when its Layer builds. Expose parsed values through a service rather than reading environment variables throughout domain code.

## Define accepted values before reading them

`Config.Literals` limits `APP_ENV` to three values. The declared default handles a missing setting.

packages/core/src/app-config.ts at 65e9465f38092e24486392f22c08f45d61230c20; lines 1-13; highlighted none.

```typescript
import { Config } from "effect";

import { ConfigService } from "./config-service.js";

export class AppConfig extends ConfigService.Service<AppConfig>()(
  "@rat-stack/core/AppConfig",
  {
    appEnv: Config.Literals(
      ["development", "test", "production"],
      "APP_ENV"
    ).pipe(Config.withDefault("development")),
  }
) {}
```

The environment name and accepted values live together. The default does not make an invalid supplied value acceptable.

Effect's `Config.schema` can describe more complex validated settings.
Use the Schema-backed path instead of writing a second parser for the same domain rule.

## Supply another configuration source

A `ConfigProvider` supplies raw configuration inputs.
Tests can replace the source with `fromUnknown` while still exercising the production parsing Layer.

packages/core/test/app-config.test.ts at 65e9465f38092e24486392f22c08f45d61230c20; lines 6-17; highlighted none.

```typescript
const withProvider = (root: Parameters<typeof ConfigProvider.fromUnknown>[0]) =>
  Layer.provide(
    AppConfig.layer,
    ConfigProvider.layer(ConfigProvider.fromUnknown(root))
  );

it.effect("reads APP_ENV through the active ConfigProvider", () =>
  Effect.gen(function* readsFromProvider() {
    const config = yield* AppConfig;
    expect(config.appEnv).toBe("test");
  }).pipe(Effect.provide(withProvider({ APP_ENV: "test" })))
);
```

The suite also checks rejection:

packages/core/test/app-config.test.ts at 65e9465f38092e24486392f22c08f45d61230c20; lines 26-34; highlighted none.

```typescript
it.effect("rejects values outside the literal set", () =>
  Effect.gen(function* rejectsUnknownLiteral() {
    const error = yield* Effect.flip(
      Layer.build(withProvider({ APP_ENV: "staging" }))
    );

    expect(error._tag).toBe("ConfigError");
  })
);
```

## Supply typed values when parsing is not the task

`AppConfig.configLayer` accepts already-typed values. It uses `Layer.succeed` and skips parsing.
Use this for a test about domain behavior. Use a provider when the test is about configuration decoding.

rat-stack's factory provides these two ways to supply configuration.

## Common wrong approach

Reading `process.env` inside each domain method ties the method to the host and allows inconsistent parsing.
A config service moves that choice to construction and gives tests a service they can replace.

Keep missing settings and rejected settings distinct. Let construction fail when a supplied value violates the schema.

## Effect idiom and house rule

- Config parses supplied data and reports typed failures. ConfigProvider selects the source.
- In rat-stack, declare environment inputs in `.env.schema`. Alchemy provider credentials come from profiles. Do not supply them through environment variables.
- Do not unwrap a redacted value for logs or public examples.

See also: [services](/lore/services-capture-dependencies), [Layer composition](/lore/layers-make-dependencies-explicit), [failures](/lore/error-model), and [tests](/lore/tests-that-earn-their-place).

Read [why dependency injection matters](/lore/dependency-injection-is-the-reason-to-choose-effect).

   Effect-TS. Config.Literals, defaults, schema validation, and capitalized Config constructors. Accessed 2026-10-06.

2. [Effect contributors. 2026. ConfigProvider. Effect 4.0.0.](https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/blob/67ba4e46a11ccda0b6761578bfd22c04ae00167d/packages/effect/src/ConfigProvider.ts)
   Effect-TS. Providers replace the config source; fromUnknown and layer support controlled inputs. Accessed 2026-10-06.

# /lore/context-and-requirements

Source: .brain/resources/lore/context-and-requirements.svx
SHA-256: 644ae8279cf7357da677eb8b9da0cfa01ab6ea72838508b773883eed6c6c0e74

# Context and requirements

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

**Goal:** read an [Effect](/lore/effect-basics) type and say which services the work still needs.

An Effect type has three parts: what the work returns, how it can fail, and which services it needs.
The third part is the requirements.
A context is the set of services that running work receives.

## Worked example: inspecting a file

rat-stack's file inspection reads a file through a `FileInspector` [service](/lore/services-capture-dependencies).
The [actor](/lore/lifecycles-are-machines) that does the read asks for that service by name:

packages/core/src/inspect-machine.ts at a3f5a14861ce89913e82bea0f7ba02c83e8d4725; lines 27-31; highlighted 29. Title: The read asks for FileInspector.

```typescript
const readStats = createEffectLogic({
  effect: ({ input }) =>
    FileInspector.use((inspector) => inspector.inspect(input.path)),
  schemas: { input: Schema.Struct({ path: Schema.String }) },
});
```

`FileInspector.use` returns an Effect whose requirements include `FileInspector`.
Nothing runs yet.
The type now records a debt: some caller must supply a `FileInspector`.

The CLI pays that debt once, at startup:

apps/cli/src/cli.ts at a3f5a14861ce89913e82bea0f7ba02c83e8d4725; lines 22-24; highlighted 24. Title: The composition root supplies it.

```typescript
  Effect.provide(
    Layer.mergeAll(
      Layer.provideMerge(FileInspector.layer, NodeServices.layer),
```

`Effect.provide` removes `FileInspector` from the requirements.
`FileInspector.layer` itself needs a file system, and `NodeServices.layer` supplies it.

The tests pay the same debt with their own Layer:

packages/core/test/inspect-machine.test.ts at a3f5a14861ce89913e82bea0f7ba02c83e8d4725; lines 14-14; highlighted none. Title: A test supplies the same requirement.

```typescript
const TestLayer = Layer.provideMerge(FileInspector.layer, NodeServices.layer);
```

The diagram above shows the same move on a small `Greeter` service: `provide` turns `Greeter` into `never`.

## Why the type carries it

The compiler rejects execution while a required service remains unsupplied. [Dependency injection](/lore/dependency-injection-is-the-reason-to-choose-effect) shows that rule.
A forgotten service fails the typecheck before the program runs.

Sam Goodwin describes this requirements channel as a way to model permissions before execution, which he calls a static effect.
He connects that idea to [Alchemy](/skills/learn-alchemy) inferring which identity and access management (IAM) policy a program needs. [Happy Path 116, 11:54](https://youtu.be/YEn4A7XxgF4?t=714)

Michael Arnaldi describes an Effect by its output, predictable failures, and requirements. [Happy Path 81, 49:15](https://youtu.be/gc5P36t6kD0?t=2955)

## Next

Read [how a service captures its dependencies](/lore/services-capture-dependencies) to see what `FileInspector` keeps inside itself.
Then read [why dependency injection matters](/lore/dependency-injection-is-the-reason-to-choose-effect).

See [Effect basics](/lore/effect-basics) for the whole type, and [infrastructure as effects](/lore/infrastructure-as-effects) for Sam's infrastructure reading.

# David Khourshid

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

David Khourshid wrote [Model-Based Testing in React with State Machines](https://css-tricks.com/model-based-testing-in-react-with-state-machines/) for CSS-Tricks in 2019. It explains how to generate tests from a state machine instead of writing each case by hand.

In the testing lesson of his Frontend Masters course on XState, he describes a test model as "a state machine, and the state machine represents all of your given when then statements in a single state machine." He adds that model-based testing lets you "test any application whether they're using state machines or not." [Testing, State Machines in JavaScript with XState, v2](https://frontendmasters.com/courses/xstate-v2/testing/)

XState is a library for defining and running state machines.
It carries that idea in `xstate/graph` with `createTestModel` and `getShortestPaths`. [Graph & Paths](https://stately.ai/docs/graph)

On 2026-10-01 he told Joel, "I need to get you on the MBT/PBT train." [X](https://x.com/davidkpiano/status/2105670489091834297) MBT means model-based testing: compare the application with a model across action sequences.
PBT means property-based testing: check rules with generated inputs.
This repo uses both: see [model-based testing](/lore/model-based-testing) and [property-based testing](/lore/property-based-testing).

2. [Testing - State Machines in JavaScript with XState, v2 | Master.dev](https://frontendmasters.com/courses/xstate-v2/testing/)
   David Khourshid · Master.dev. Testing lesson; used for the XState testing course reference. Accessed 2026-10-01.

3. [Graph & Paths](https://stately.ai/docs/graph)
   David Khourshid · Stately docs. Path generation docs; used for createTestModel and getShortestPaths. Accessed 2026-10-01.

# /lore/dead-letters-need-a-return-path

Source: .brain/resources/lore/dead-letters-need-a-return-path.svx
SHA-256: 0a1280ba9ff44c1eb96223e881a3f5612536add7f1dd4202787afb069ed1506f

# Dead letters need a return path

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Partial batch failure needs a decision about failed records and successful siblings. Parking work is a recovery boundary. It does not prove successful processing.

> Do you put the failed event into a DLQ and process it later?

Source: [Q20](/lore/durability-bibliography#q20); [B5](/lore/durability-bibliography#b5-building-event-driven-microservices), [B9](/lore/durability-bibliography#b9-serverless-architectures-on-aws).

## Failure it prevents

A failed item disappears, blocks useful work, or causes successful siblings to run repeatedly.

## Our Effect 4.0.0 reading

`PersistedQueue` retains failed records. `DurableQueue` exhaustion can leave its `DurableDeferred` unresolved and the workflow parked. Provide out-of-band repair and requeue.

Source: `packages/effect/src/persistence/PersistedQueue.ts`, `packages/effect/src/workflow/DurableQueue.ts`.

## How to check

Exhaust an item, find its failure record, repair it, and prove redrive resumes the intended waiter without repeating successful siblings. This check is our proposal. The books do not prescribe it.

Continue with [Retry needs idempotent effects](/lore/retry-needs-idempotency), [Golden signals expose overload](/lore/golden-signals-expose-overload).

Connect this to [the existing rat-stack guidance](/lore/concurrent-work-needs-an-owner).

Use [the durability skill](/skills/durability) for the full review. Return to [the durability index](/lore/durability).

## Sources

1. [Bellemare, Adam. Building Event-Driven Microservices: Leveraging Organizational Data at Scale. O’Reilly, 2020.](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/building-event-driven-microservices/9781492057888/)
   O’Reilly. Chapter 3 Communication and Data Contracts; Chapter 6 Deterministic Stream Processing; Chapter 7 Stateful Streaming; Chapter 9 Microservices Using Function-as-a-Service; Chapter 14 Supportive Tooling. Accessed 2026-10-23.

2. [Sbarski, Peter; Cui, Yan; Nair, Ajay. Serverless Architectures on AWS, Second Edition.](https://www.manning.com/books/serverless-architectures-on-aws-second-edition)
   Manning. Chapter 6, The New Search Microservice: Everything Fails, All the Time; Pay Attention to Retry Configurations. AWS-specific mechanisms are not universal runtime guarantees. Accessed 2026-10-23.

3. [Effect contributors. Effect 4.0.0. persistence/PersistedQueue.ts](https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/blob/67ba4e46a11ccda0b6761578bfd22c04ae00167d/packages/effect/src/persistence/PersistedQueue.ts)
   Effect-TS. Pinned source for our Effect mapping, not a claim from the book. Accessed 2026-10-23.

4. [Effect contributors. Effect 4.0.0. workflow/DurableQueue.ts](https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/blob/67ba4e46a11ccda0b6761578bfd22c04ae00167d/packages/effect/src/workflow/DurableQueue.ts)
   Effect-TS. Pinned source for our Effect mapping, not a claim from the book. Accessed 2026-10-23.

# /lore/dependency-injection-is-the-reason-to-choose-effect

Source: .brain/resources/lore/dependency-injection-is-the-reason-to-choose-effect.svx
SHA-256: bbc4320993750918ef649d4c7db2da27ab9f58ff09e5963c280ee9dcdc8e8069

# Dependency injection is the reason to choose Effect

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Matt Pocock puts dependency injection first:

> Now, what I think people get wrong is that they think that error handling and the type-safe nature of Effect is the reason you go for Effect. I think the reason you go for Effect is dependency injection, actually. It allows you to create these beautiful small modules that you can just swap out as needed and create these really nice looking tests with Effect too.

Dillon Mulroy compares Effect with Spring and NestJS:

> Effect has probably the most novel dependency injection system that I've worked with. I've worked in enterprise languages like Java, done the whole Spring system. I've worked with NestJS. Effect's dependency injection is genuinely fantastic and really, really nice to work with.

[Watch Dillon's one-minute clip](https://player.mux.com/nB8qFbdBBHVU6zUfXsbtHFR2tKgEnjYEiPd4bL4Jny4).

## Requirements stay visible

An `Effect<A, E, R>` describes its result, failure, and required services. The `R` type tracks those requirements. The compiler rejects execution while a required service remains in `R`.

A service gives callers a typed interface. A Layer builds its implementation and declares its construction requirements. Shared Layer identity reuses construction within the same memoization context.

## A service captures its dependencies

`FileInspector.make` obtains `FileSystem` during construction. Its `inspect` method uses that captured service. The method's type carries no filesystem requirement.

packages/core/src/file-inspector.ts at c39e106e33eaa00432454ed31c59fa90389255d0; lines 6-16; highlighted none. Title: FileInspector captures FileSystem.

```typescript
export class FileInspector extends Context.Service<
  FileInspector,
  {
    readonly inspect: (
      path: string
    ) => Effect.Effect<FileStats, FileStatsError>;
  }
>()("@rat-stack/core/FileInspector", {
  make: Effect.gen(function* makeFileInspector() {
    const fileSystem = yield* FileSystem.FileSystem;

```

The static Layer builds the service through `make`.

packages/core/src/file-inspector.ts at c39e106e33eaa00432454ed31c59fa90389255d0; lines 17-35; highlighted none. Title: The inspection method and static Layer.

```typescript
    const inspect = Effect.fn("FileInspector.inspect")(function* inspect(
      path: string
    ) {
      const content = yield* fileSystem
        .readFile(path)
        .pipe(
          Effect.mapError(
            (error) => new FileStatsError({ path, reason: error.message })
          )
        );

      return summarizeBytes(path, content);
    });

    return { inspect } as const;
  }),
}) {
  static readonly layer = Layer.effect(this, this.make);
}
```

## Tests supply another implementation

The inspection model test supplies a controlled `FileInspector`. Its fake waits for a result chosen by the test. One `provideService` replaces the implementation.

packages/core/test/inspect-machine.model.test.ts at c39e106e33eaa00432454ed31c59fa90389255d0; lines 125-135; highlighted none. Title: A controlled FileInspector.

```typescript
  const inspector = FileInspector.of({
    inspect: (path) => {
      requested.push(path);

      return Deferred.await(result);
    },
  });

  const actor = yield* createEffectActor(inspectMachine, {
    input: { path: scenario.stats.path },
  }).pipe(Effect.provideService(FileInspector, inspector));
```

`Effect.provide` supplies a Layer or Context. `Effect.provideService` supplies one service directly. Both remove the supplied service from the requirements type.

# Alchemy and the next generation of infrastructure as code

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Sam argues that infrastructure tools have accumulated layers around provider APIs. Alchemy reduces the resource model to stateful TypeScript functions with create, update, delete, tests, consistency checks, and idempotent recovery.
Idempotent recovery can repeat an operation without creating another change. [04:09](https://youtu.be/babOa4shATk?t=249) [06:01](https://youtu.be/babOa4shATk?t=361) [12:13](https://youtu.be/babOa4shATk?t=733)

He says constrained conventions make resource generation easier for coding agents. He also describes embedding the runtime in Durable Objects and workflows. [33:00](https://youtu.be/babOa4shATk?t=1980) [25:38](https://youtu.be/babOa4shATk?t=1538)

# Double opt-in

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

With [double opt-in](https://github.com/joelhooks/rat-stack/blob/main/.brain/archives/projects/tokenmaxx-interest-form.svx), the visitor gets one confirmation email. They count only after using its link.

GET is the HTTP method for reading a page.
The link opens a page with a button because:

> Mail scanners follow links, and a GET that confirms would count a scanner as a person.

# /lore/durability-bibliography

Source: .brain/resources/lore/durability-bibliography.svx
SHA-256: 0d751911dc088f62fad2d472fc3aee6b042331153ce29ade40f2281eaae13def

# Durability bibliography

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Book principles and our [Effect](/lore/effect-basics) mappings are separate. Each entry names the book and the chapters or sections we read. Unknown edition details stay unknown. Quote numbers match the links on the durability pages.

## Books

### B1 Erlang and OTP in Action

Logan, Martin; Merritt, Eric; Carlsson, Richard. *Erlang and OTP in Action*.

**Read:**

- The Erlang/OTP Platform: Let It Crash
- process isolation
- §4.2.2 supervisor restart strategy

**Edition:** Edition, publisher, and year are not confirmed.

[Public book reference](https://www.manning.com/books/erlang-and-otp-in-action).

#### Q01

> The point of letting an entire subsystem terminate and be restarted is that it brings you back to a state known to function properly.

### B2 Elixir in Action

Jurić, Saša. *Elixir in Action*, Third Edition. Manning, 2024.

**Read:**

- §5.4.3 Shared-Nothing Concurrency
- Chapters 8–9, fault tolerance and supervision
- Other Use Cases for ETS

[Public book reference](https://www.manning.com/books/elixir-in-action-third-edition).

#### Q02

> Remember from chapters 8 and 9 that processes lose their state on termination.

#### Q03

> Shared-nothing concurrency ensures complete isolation between processes: one process can’t compromise the internal state of another.

### B3 Designing Elixir Systems with OTP

Gray II, James Edward; Tate, Bruce A. *Designing Elixir Systems with OTP*. Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2019.

**Read:**

- Build a Functional Core
- Isolate Process Machinery in a Boundary
- Customize Your Lifecycle
- Big, Loud Worker-Bees
- Add Persistence as a Boundary [Service](/lore/services-capture-dependencies)
- Test the Boundary

**Edition:** Not stated.

[Public book reference](https://pragprog.com/titles/jgotp/designing-elixir-systems-with-otp/).

#### Q04

> Elixir can’t manage what it doesn’t know about.

#### Q14

> Our core doesn’t access external interfaces or use any process machinery your component might use.

### B4 Release It

Nygard, Michael T. *Release It!: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software*. Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2007.

**Read:**

- §4.4 Unbounded Result Sets
- Chapter 5 Stability Patterns
- §5.1 Timeouts
- §5.2 [Circuit Breaker](/lore/circuit-breakers-have-state)
- §5.3 Bulkheads
- §5.4 Steady State
- §5.5 Fail Fast
- §5.6 Handshaking
- §5.7 Test Harness
- §5.8 Decoupling Middleware

**Edition:** Not stated. Do not substitute second-edition chapter numbering.

[Public book reference](https://archive.org/details/releaseitdesignd0000nyga).

#### Q05

> The timeout is a simple mechanism allowing you to stop waiting for an answer once you think it will not come.

#### Q06

> calls to the circuit breaker fail immediately, without any attempt to execute the real operation.

#### Q07

> Protect critical clients by giving them their own pool to call.

#### Q08

> The Steady State pattern says, for every mechanism that accumulates a resource, some other mechanism must recycle that resource.

#### Q09

> The Test Harness can produce slow responses, no responses, or garbage responses.

### B5 Building Event-Driven Microservices

Bellemare, Adam. *Building Event-Driven Microservices: Leveraging Organizational Data at Scale*. O’Reilly, 2020.

**Read:**

- Chapter 3 Communication and Data Contracts
- Chapter 6 Deterministic Stream Processing
- Chapter 7 Stateful Streaming
- Chapter 9 Microservices Using Function-as-a-Service
- Chapter 14 Supportive Tooling

**Edition:** Not stated. Quotes come from the 2020 text.

[Public book reference](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/building-event-driven-microservices/9781492057888/).

#### Q11

> The overarching goal of deterministic processing is that a microservice should produce the same output whether it is processing in real time or catching up to the present time.

#### Q12

> Schema evolution ensures that the consumer can translate it to a familiar version.

#### Q13

> allowing a single stateful transaction to atomically update both the state and input offsets.

### B6 Fundamentals of Data Engineering

Reis, Joe; Housley, Matt. *Fundamentals of Data Engineering*. O’Reilly.

**Read:**

- Part II, Chapter 5: Message Queues
- DataOps considerations
- Incident Response

**Edition:** Edition and year are not confirmed.

[Public book reference](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/fundamentals-of-data/9781098108298).

#### Q10

> In an idempotent system, the outcome of processing a message once is identical to the outcome of processing it multiple times.

### B7 Domain Modeling Made Functional

Wlaschin, Scott. *Domain Modeling Made Functional: Tackle Software Complexity with Domain-Driven Design and F#*. Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2018.

**Read:**

- Implementation: Working with Errors
- Using the Result Type to Make Errors Explicit
- Handling Exceptions
- Composing in Parallel with Applicatives

**Edition:** Printing P1.0. The numbered edition is not stated.

[Public book reference](https://pragprog.com/titles/swdddf/domain-modeling-made-functional/).

#### Q15

> These different kinds of errors require different implementations.

### B8 Monitoring Distributed Systems

Ewaschuk, Rob. *Monitoring Distributed Systems*. O’Reilly, 2016.

**Read:**

- The Four Golden Signals
- Black-Box Versus White-Box
- Symptoms Versus Causes

**Edition:** First edition. It is also a chapter of the Google SRE book.

[Public book reference](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/).

#### Q18

> The four golden signals of monitoring are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.

### B9 Serverless Architectures on AWS

Sbarski, Peter; Cui, Yan; Nair, Ajay. *Serverless Architectures on AWS*, Second Edition.

**Read:**

- Chapter 6, The New Search Microservice: Everything Fails, All the Time
- Pay Attention to Retry Configurations

AWS-specific mechanisms are not universal runtime guarantees.

**Edition:** Publisher and year are not confirmed.

[Public book reference](https://www.manning.com/books/serverless-architectures-on-aws-second-edition).

#### Q20

> Do you put the failed event into a DLQ and process it later?

### B10 A Philosophy of Software Design

Ousterhout, John. *A Philosophy of Software Design*. 2018.

**Read:**

- §4.4 Deep Modules
- §10.2 Too Many Exceptions
- §10.3 Define Errors Out of Existence
- §10.6 Mask Exceptions
- §10.7 Exception Aggregation
- §10.8 Just Crash?
- §10.10 Taking It Too Far

**Edition:** Edition and publisher are not confirmed.

[Public book reference](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/book.php).

#### Q16

> Rather than throwing an error when unset is asked to delete an unknown variable, it should have simply returned without doing anything.

### B11 Property-Based Testing

Hebert, Fred. *Property-Based Testing with PropEr, Erlang, and Elixir*. Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2019.

**Read:**

- Chapter 7 Shrinking
- Laying Out Stateful Properties
- Testing Parallel Executions
- Initial State for the State Machine
- Adjusting the Model

Use the actual breaker’s threshold semantics.

**Edition:** Not stated.

[Public book reference](https://pragprog.com/titles/fhproper/property-based-testing-with-proper-erlang-and-elixir/).

#### Q17

> Both function calls must be deterministic.

### B12 Site Reliability Engineering

Beyer, Betsy; Jones, Chris; Petoff, Jennifer; Murphy, Niall Richard, editors. *Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems*. O’Reilly, 2016.

**Read:**

- Chapter 3 Embracing Risk
- Chapter 22 Addressing Cascading Failures (Mike Ulrich)
- Chapter 26 General Principles of SRE as Applied to Data Integrity
- Chapter 27 Reliable Product Launches at Scale

Section-only excerpts limit detailed attribution.

**Edition:** Not stated.

[Public book reference](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/).

### B13 Grokking Simplicity

Normand, Eric. *Grokking Simplicity: Taming Complex Software with Functional Thinking*. Manning, 2021.

**Read:**

- Chapters 15–17: Isolating Timelines, Sharing Resources Between Timelines, Coordinating Timelines

**Edition:** Not stated.

[Public book reference](https://www.manning.com/books/grokking-simplicity).

### B14 Refactoring Databases

Ambler, Scott W.; Sadalage, Pramod J. *Refactoring Databases: Evolutionary Database Design*. Addison-Wesley, 2006.

**Read:**

- §3.11 What You Have Learned (transition period)
- Chapter 4 Deploying into Production

**Edition:** Not stated.

[Public book reference](https://www.amazon.com/Refactoring-Databases-Evolutionary-paperback-Addison-Wesley/dp/0321774515).

#### Q19

> many refactorings require you to run both the original and new versions of the schema in parallel during a transition period that is long enough to allow any applications accessing that portion of the schema time to be redeployed.

### B15 Software Engineering at Google

Winters, Titus; Manshreck, Tom; Wright, Hyrum, editors. *Software Engineering at Google: Lessons Learned from Programming Over Time*. O’Reilly, 2020.

**Read:**

- Chapter 15 Deprecation: Deprecation Tooling and Preventing Backsliding
- CI Is Alerting (hermetic and flaky tests)

**Edition:** Not stated.

[Public book reference](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book).

### B16 Why Programs Fail

Zeller, Andreas. *Why Programs Fail: A Guide to Systematic Debugging*. Morgan Kaufmann, 2009.

**Read:**

- Chapter 4 Reproducing the Problem Environment
- Chapter 10 Reference Runs

Short section excerpts do not establish a complete debugging method.

**Edition:** Not stated.

## Coverage limits

Some books gave no usable passage for this topic:

- *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* and Newman’s *Building Microservices* gave only fragments for their [scope](/lore/scopes-own-resources).
- *Adopting Elixir* and *Programming Elixir* gave no usable findings.
- The Scala text gave no usable passage.

These pages make no book-backed claims about fencing, consensus, compensation, or replication. They add no hot-upgrade or Governor rule.

## Effect source

Effect contributors. *Effect*, `effect@4.0.0`, commit `67ba4e46a11ccda0b6761578bfd22c04ae00167d`. See [the durability skill](/skills/durability) and its [reference copy of this bibliography](https://github.com/joelhooks/rat-stack/blob/main/skills/durability/references/bibliography.md). All mappings and proposed checks are our own reading of the books.

Return to [the durability index](/lore/durability).

# Durability starts with a recovery record

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

**Effect is not BEAM.** Fibers do not provide private process heaps or OTP restart strategies. A durable operation needs storage and a recovery owner.

Use [the durability skill](/skills/durability) to review a design. [The durability system page](/systems/durability) shows the patterns rat-stack ships. These pages separate the book principles from our Effect API mappings.

The mappings were written and checked against Effect 4.0.0. The template now pins Effect 4.1.2, and the mappings have not been re-audited against it. Check your own Effect [pin](/skills/gardener) before you apply a mapping.

## Reading order

- [Effect is not BEAM](/lore/effect-is-not-beam): Fibers share a runtime; [scope](/lore/scopes-own-resources) ownership does not supply isolated heaps or OTP restart strategies.
- [Durable work needs storage](/lore/durable-work-needs-storage): A restarted worker cannot recover intent that existed only in memory.
- [Every task needs an owner](/lore/every-task-needs-an-owner): Give child work a lifetime, a failure observer, and a recovery decision.
- [Supervision chooses what restarts](/lore/supervision-is-a-recovery-policy): Restart policy follows dependency shape and bounds repeated recovery.
- [Restart must reconstruct known state](/lore/restart-from-known-state): Execution recovery and state recovery need separate contracts.
- [Retry needs idempotent effects](/lore/retry-needs-idempotency): Repeating an operation must preserve its intended observable result.
- [Checkpoints follow the promised commit](/lore/checkpoints-follow-commits): Persist state and progress together when one store can transact both.
- [Replay needs stable inputs](/lore/replay-needs-stable-inputs): Historical processing must not silently depend on today’s clock or external decisions.
- [Old events must still decode](/lore/old-events-must-still-decode): Retained data needs compatibility rules before recovery depends on it.
- [Dead letters need a return path](/lore/dead-letters-need-a-return-path): Exhausted work needs durable evidence, an owner, and deliberate redrive.
- [Timeouts bound waiting](/lore/timeouts-bound-waiting): A local timeout stops waiting; it does not prove the remote action never happened.
- [Retry load needs a budget](/lore/retry-load-needs-a-budget): One retry owner must control attempts, delay, and aggregate load.
- [Circuit breakers have state](/lore/circuit-breakers-have-state): A breaker stops doomed calls and controls probes before restoring traffic.
- [Bulkheads isolate scarce capacity](/lore/bulkheads-isolate-capacity): Reserve independent capacity for workloads that must not starve each other.
- [Backpressure reaches the producer](/lore/backpressure-reaches-the-producer): Bounded consumption helps only when upstream respects waiting or refusal.
- [Admission control protects recovery](/lore/admission-controls-new-work): Refuse or defer work that cannot be served usefully under current load.
- [Steady state recycles resources](/lore/steady-state-recycles-resources): Every accumulation needs a deliberate recycling policy.
- [Queries need result bounds](/lore/queries-need-result-bounds): Limit result cardinality before the driver materializes an oversized response.
- [Failures keep their meaning](/lore/failures-keep-their-meaning): Expected refusals, infrastructure faults, and defects need different policies.
- [Cleanup can be an idempotent postcondition](/lore/cleanup-can-be-an-idempotent-postcondition): Already-absent state can be success when absence is the operation’s intended result.
- [Pure cores reduce timeline coupling](/lore/pure-cores-reduce-timelines): Move deterministic rules out of time-dependent actions and shared mutable state.
- [Recovery needs model tests](/lore/recovery-needs-model-tests): Test sequences of failures and recoveries against explicit invariants.
- [Golden signals expose overload](/lore/golden-signals-expose-overload): Measure latency, traffic, errors, and saturation, including failed work.
- [Shared schemas need a transition period](/lore/schema-changes-need-a-transition): Keep old and new representations usable while consumers migrate.
- [Durable timers need recovery](/lore/durable-timers-need-recovery): Persist scheduled intent when losing a worker must not lose its deadlines.
- [Request lifetime is not durability](/lore/request-lifetime-is-not-durability): Worker `waitUntil` has a shared post-response allowance; required work needs a durable marker and redrive.

# Durable timers need recovery

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

A crashed server loses timers that existed only in memory. Decide whether to restore scheduled work and identify its durable recovery data.

Book basis: [B3](/lore/durability-bibliography#b3-designing-elixir-systems-with-otp).

## Failure it prevents

A scheduler restarts but pending deadlines silently disappear.

## Our Effect 4.0.0 reading

`DurableClock` and `DurableDeferred` cooperate with `WorkflowEngine`. For an existing storage/alarm owner, keep scheduling in that [adapter](/lore/hexagonal-architecture). A `Schedule` loop alone is not persistence.

Source: `packages/effect/src/workflow/DurableClock.ts`, `packages/effect/src/workflow/DurableDeferred.ts`, `packages/effect/src/workflow/WorkflowEngine.ts`, `packages/effect/src/Schedule.ts`.

## How to check

Crash before the deadline. Recover it from storage and test both wakeup and cancellation. This check is our proposal. The books do not prescribe it.

Continue with [Durable work needs storage](/lore/durable-work-needs-storage), [Restart must reconstruct known state](/lore/restart-from-known-state).

Connect this to [the existing rat-stack guidance](/lore/lifecycles-are-machines).

# Durable work needs storage

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

A running server and a recovery record solve different problems. Choose what must survive termination and how the next worker finds it.

> Remember from chapters 8 and 9 that processes lose their state on termination.

Source: [Q02](/lore/durability-bibliography#q02); [B2](/lore/durability-bibliography#b2-elixir-in-action), [B3](/lore/durability-bibliography#b3-designing-elixir-systems-with-otp).

## Failure it prevents

The [service](/lore/services-capture-dependencies) restarts successfully while accepted work disappears.

## Our Effect 4.0.0 reading

`Workflow`, `Activity`, and `WorkflowEngine` describe resumable work. Choose persistent engine storage. `WorkflowEngine.layerMemory` keeps state only in memory.

Source: `packages/effect/src/workflow/Workflow.ts`, `packages/effect/src/workflow/Activity.ts`, `packages/effect/src/workflow/WorkflowEngine.ts`.

## How to check

Kill the worker after acceptance. Recover the same operation identity from the selected backend. This check is our proposal. The books do not prescribe it.

Continue with [Every task needs an owner](/lore/every-task-needs-an-owner), [Checkpoints follow the promised commit](/lore/checkpoints-follow-commits).

Connect this to [the existing rat-stack guidance](/lore/concurrent-work-needs-an-owner).

# /lore/effect-basics

Source: .brain/resources/lore/effect-basics.svx
SHA-256: 6b25c60dd3505e3c8688fe3402d4849681d72ca19fad5aaa662188ed4226bcb5

# Effect basics

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

A service is a named interface for work. A context holds supplied service implementations.

An Effect describes work. Build the description, compose it with other Effects, supply its services, then let a runtime execute it.

## Read the three type parameters

`Effect.Effect<A, E, R>` describes three things:

- **`A`**:
  - Meaning: Success value
  - FileInspector's inspect method: `FileStats`
- **`E`**:
  - Meaning: Expected failure
  - FileInspector's inspect method: `FileStatsError`
- **`R`**:
  - Meaning: Required services
  - FileInspector's inspect method: `never`

This method's full return type is `Effect.Effect<FileStats, FileStatsError, never>`.
The source omits the final parameter because it defaults to `never`.

packages/core/src/file-inspector.ts at 65e9465f38092e24486392f22c08f45d61230c20; lines 6-15; highlighted none.

```typescript
export class FileInspector extends Context.Service<
  FileInspector,
  {
    readonly inspect: (
      path: string
    ) => Effect.Effect<FileStats, FileStatsError>;
  }
>()("@rat-stack/core/FileInspector", {
  make: Effect.gen(function* makeFileInspector() {
    const fileSystem = yield* FileSystem.FileSystem;
```

Constructing the inspector needs `FileSystem`. Its returned method has captured that dependency and does not require it again.

`R = never` means no services remain to supply. It does not mean the computation cannot fail.
`E = never` means no declared expected failures; it does not rule out defects or interruption.

## A description is not a completed operation

Calling `inspector.inspect(path)` produces an Effect description. It does not read the file immediately.
The method composes the read with an error translation before a runtime executes either operation.

packages/core/src/file-inspector.ts at 65e9465f38092e24486392f22c08f45d61230c20; lines 17-29; highlighted none.

```typescript
    const inspect = Effect.fn("FileInspector.inspect")(function* inspect(
      path: string
    ) {
      const content = yield* fileSystem
        .readFile(path)
        .pipe(
          Effect.mapError(
            (error) => new FileStatsError({ path, reason: error.message })
          )
        );

      return summarizeBytes(path, content);
    });
```

Ordinary JavaScript still evaluates while you build a description.
Starting a Promise first, then wrapping it, does not undo that eager work.
Keep external work inside the Effect constructor's callback.

## Write a sequence with gen; transform it with pipe

`Effect.gen` composes Effects in generator syntax. `yield*` obtains a success value or propagates the failure.
The generator describes work for the Effect runtime.

Use `pipe` for short transforms, such as mapping a value, translating a failure, or providing a service.
Use a generator when the next step needs values from earlier steps.

- Combinators are functions that combine or transform Effects.

Generators and combinators both compose descriptions without running a nested runtime.

- In rat-stack, prefer `Effect.gen` for inline sequences. Use `Effect.fn` for reusable functions with useful tracing names.
- Do not write long combinator chains merely to avoid a clear generator.

## Expected failures and defects are different

An [expected failure](/lore/error-model) belongs in `E`, where callers can handle it by its declared type or tag.
A defect is an unexpected execution failure.
Logging a failure does not make the operation successful.
[Handle expected failures without hiding defects](/lore/error-model) shows the file error and its CLI handler.

## Requirements name services to supply

A requirement is a service the computation needs.
A Layer describes how to build a service and supply its dependencies.

Layers build implementations and satisfy their construction dependencies.
Getting `FileInspector` from context requires that service; calling its captured `inspect` method needs no extra service.
Read [service construction](/lore/services-capture-dependencies), [Layer composition](/lore/layers-make-dependencies-explicit), and [context and requirements](/lore/context-and-requirements).

## Run at the application boundary

The CLI builds and transforms a program with `pipe`, then provides its services and their dependencies.
`NodeRuntime.runMain` executes the final Effect:

apps/cli/src/cli.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 22-35; highlighted none.

```typescript
  Effect.provide(
    Layer.mergeAll(
      Layer.provideMerge(FileInspector.layer, NodeServices.layer),
      remoteJoinInterestLayer,
      localPromptLibraryLayer.pipe(Layer.provide(NodeServices.layer)),
      localCafeDirectoryLayer.pipe(Layer.provide(NodeServices.layer)),
      localLearnLayer,
      Flags.defaults(eventFlags),
      Approval.denyAll
    )
  )
);

NodeRuntime.runMain(program);
```

The Worker returns a fetch Effect to its Alchemy Worker adapter:

apps/site/src/worker.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 337-342,357-365; highlighted none.

```typescript
    return {
      fetch: observeRequestLog(
        observeRequestIncidents(
          events === undefined
            ? readerApp
            : Effect.gen(function* captureWithLiveIdentity() {
                return yield* withEventCapture({
                  captureCity: true,
                  identityMode: currentIdentity,
                  runInBackground: inBackground,
                })(readerApp).pipe(Effect.provideContext(events));
              })
        )
      ),
    };
```

The Worker adapter owns request execution. The domain does not scatter `runPromise` calls through handlers.

In tests, `it.effect` owns execution of the returned Effect. The test still supplies the services it needs.
See [tests through supplied services](/lore/tests-that-earn-their-place).
[Run Effect at the integration boundary](/lore/run-effect-at-the-boundary) covers foreign code, runtime reuse, and disposal.

## The common wrong first version

Scattering `await Effect.runPromise(...)` through library methods creates separate execution boundaries where composition should remain intact.
It also turns the expected failure into a rejected Promise rather than preserving the Effect error channel for the caller.
Return the composed Effect and let the application boundary run it.

`Effect.promise` assumes Promise rejection is an unexpected defect.
For an external API with expected failures, use `Effect.tryPromise` with a translation into a named domain error.
Wrapping an already-started Promise also loses control over when its work begins.

Michael describes Effect 4 as a review of choices made in Effect 3, driven by production feedback. The work aims to remove duplicate concepts, reduce bundle size, and improve core data types. # Effect's design lineage

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Dependency injection supplies service implementations to the code that needs them.
Resource safety means cleaning up resources after use. Concurrency control manages work that runs at the same time.

Michael traces the first Effect implementation to a team's need for dependency injection, tests, resource safety, concurrency control, and retries in TypeScript. [Effect Days 2024, 08:40](https://youtu.be/7sJc3Z4mh1w?t=520).

ZIO is a Scala library for describing effects.
John De Goes describes Effect as adapting ZIO's goals to TypeScript through iterations rather than copying it directly. [Cause & Effect 10, 48:01](https://youtu.be/irmz5X3c7Do?t=2881) [49:49](https://youtu.be/irmz5X3c7Do?t=2989).

See [Effect Days 2024](/lore/effect-days-2024-origin-story-michael-arnaldi) and [Cause & Effect 10](/lore/cause-and-effect-10-software-engineering-age-of-ai-de-goes).

# /lore/effect-is-not-beam

Source: .brain/resources/lore/effect-is-not-beam.svx
SHA-256: 7404f094e23db2b1b29b2e0cb8d2ab7324eef2b315a253689bc8bd2e95ee7713

# Effect is not BEAM

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

BEAM processes isolate their state. Supervision observes worker failure and applies restart policy. Restart still loses volatile state.

> Shared-nothing concurrency ensures complete isolation between processes: one process can’t compromise the internal state of another.

Source: [Q03](/lore/durability-bibliography#q03); [B1](/lore/durability-bibliography#b1-erlang-and-otp-in-action), [B2](/lore/durability-bibliography#b2-elixir-in-action), [B3](/lore/durability-bibliography#b3-designing-elixir-systems-with-otp).

## Failure it prevents

A failed computation has already changed shared state, while the caller assumes process isolation.

## Our Effect 4.0.0 reading

[Scope](/lore/scopes-own-resources) and `FiberSet` own local lifetimes. They do not supply separate heaps or OTP restart strategies. Use a host boundary for hard isolation.

Source: `packages/effect/src/Scope.ts`, `packages/effect/src/FiberSet.ts`, `packages/effect/src/Fiber.ts`.

## How to check

State which failure the boundary contains. Test a worker [defect](/lore/effect-basics) and a hard runtime exit separately. This check is our proposal. The books do not prescribe it.

Continue with [Supervision chooses what restarts](/lore/supervision-is-a-recovery-policy), [Durable work needs storage](/lore/durable-work-needs-storage).

Connect this to [the existing rat-stack guidance](/lore/concurrent-work-needs-an-owner).

Use [the durability skill](/skills/durability) for the full review. Return to [the durability index](/lore/durability).

## Sources

1. [Logan, Martin; Merritt, Eric; Carlsson, Richard. Erlang and OTP in Action.](https://www.manning.com/books/erlang-and-otp-in-action)
   Manning. The Erlang/OTP Platform: Let It Crash; process isolation; §4.2.2 supervisor restart strategy. Accessed 2026-10-23.

2. [Jurić, Saša. Elixir in Action, Third Edition. Manning, 2024.](https://www.manning.com/books/elixir-in-action-third-edition)
   Manning. §5.4.3 Shared-Nothing Concurrency; Chapters 8–9, fault tolerance and supervision; Other Use Cases for ETS. Accessed 2026-10-23.

3. [Gray II, James Edward; Tate, Bruce A. Designing Elixir Systems with OTP. Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2019.](https://pragprog.com/titles/jgotp/designing-elixir-systems-with-otp/)
   Pragmatic Bookshelf. Build a Functional Core; Isolate Process Machinery in a Boundary; Customize Your Lifecycle; Big, Loud Worker-Bees; Add Persistence as a Boundary Service; Test the Boundary. Accessed 2026-10-23.

4. [Effect contributors. Effect 4.0.0. Scope.ts](https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/blob/67ba4e46a11ccda0b6761578bfd22c04ae00167d/packages/effect/src/Scope.ts)
   Effect-TS. Pinned source for our Effect mapping, not a claim from the book. Accessed 2026-10-23.

5. [Effect contributors. Effect 4.0.0. FiberSet.ts](https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/blob/67ba4e46a11ccda0b6761578bfd22c04ae00167d/packages/effect/src/FiberSet.ts)
   Effect-TS. Pinned source for our Effect mapping, not a claim from the book. Accessed 2026-10-23.

   Effect-TS. Pinned source for our Effect mapping, not a claim from the book. Accessed 2026-10-23.

Michael presents Effect as a missing standard library for TypeScript, bringing typed errors and requirements, structured concurrency, observability, resource safety, and composition into one runtime. [01:44](https://youtu.be/BqUnsDnMnMo?t=104) [02:31](https://youtu.be/BqUnsDnMnMo?t=151)

Structured concurrency gives child work an owner that controls when it stops.
Observability uses logs, metrics, and traces to understand a running system.

A Remix demo contrasts manually added logs, metrics, and traces and nested error handling with Effect context, Schema, spans, metrics, and retry policies. [22:37](https://youtu.be/BqUnsDnMnMo?t=1357) [30:34](https://youtu.be/BqUnsDnMnMo?t=1834)

# Effect Office Hours 27: Alchemy, infrastructure as effects

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Sam describes a workflow for coding agents from an empty project through deployment, tests, CI, and operations.
An Effect describes work with typed failures and required services.
A Layer describes how to build services and supply their dependencies.
An Alchemy Stack is the infrastructure program that declares cloud resources.

Effects and Layers let the type system track the resource providers a Stack needs.
Tests using real infrastructure check behavior after deployment. [03:38](https://youtu.be/fPSxB7ZgSJw?t=218) [07:01](https://youtu.be/fPSxB7ZgSJw?t=421) [16:01](https://youtu.be/fPSxB7ZgSJw?t=961)

He explains bindings as application capabilities that can inform least-privilege policies, which limit permissions to the application methods in use. The runtime and infrastructure stay related without bundling provider implementations into the application. [58:16](https://youtu.be/fPSxB7ZgSJw?t=3496) [59:23](https://youtu.be/fPSxB7ZgSJw?t=3563) [70:55](https://youtu.be/fPSxB7ZgSJw?t=4255)

Source: .brain/resources/lore/engine-neutral-tokens-keep-adapters-replaceable.svx

# Engine-neutral tokens keep adapters replaceable

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

A highlighter port is an interface for highlighting code, independent of the chosen highlighting tool.
This follows [ports and adapters](/lore/hexagonal-architecture).

The [code-snippets design brief](/lore/code-snippets) specifies an engine-neutral token:

- `text`: token source text.
- `role`: syntax role.
- `fontStyle`: style information.

The highlighter port also exposes languages, aliases, themes, and an engine fingerprint.
This identifier records the highlighter, version, and settings used in token cache keys.

The proposed Shiki adapter keeps Shiki's token type inside the adapter.
A plain adapter returns uncoloured text.
Both adapters provide the same port through an [Effect Layer](/lore/layer-constructor-pattern).

Core properties use the plain adapter.
The whole-file token property exercises Shiki.
[One snippet model](/lore/one-snippet-model-two-renderers) supplies both renderers.

See [the glossary](/glossary) for engine-neutral token and highlighter port.

   Primary source. Proposed highlighter contract Accessed 2026-10-02.

# /lore/error-model

Source: .brain/resources/lore/error-model.svx
SHA-256: 9b25ffa54d4addbb6ef4e2e639750db5c4bc62bbc11ce65378e0104e87a447f2

# Handle expected failures without hiding defects

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

A defect is an unexpected execution failure.

Declare failures that callers can handle. Keep defects distinct from those declared outcomes.
Catch a failure where the application can recover or report it truthfully.

## Give expected failures a type and useful context

`Schema.TaggedError` defines a yieldable error: an error a generator can raise with `yield*`.
Its tag identifies the error type; its fields retain context.
`FileStatsError` keeps the path and the filesystem reason.
The brand stops two classes with the same fields from being assignable to each other.

packages/core/src/stats.ts at c936b94c957ada7199df3ab7b39a330d6e1c644f; lines 13-26; highlighted none.

```typescript
export class FileStatsError extends Schema.TaggedError<
  FileStatsError,
  { readonly brand: unique symbol }
>()("FileStatsError", {
  path: Schema.String,
  reason: Schema.String,
}) {
  override readonly [Runtime.errorExitCode] = 1;
  override readonly [Runtime.errorReported] = false;

  override get message(): string {
    return `Could not read ${this.path}: ${this.reason}`;
  }
}
```

Inside a generator, `return yield*` can raise a yieldable error directly.
`Effect.fail` can also place an error in the expected failure channel, the `E` parameter of the Effect type.
Do not throw an ordinary exception to represent a declared refusal.

## Translate implementation failures without losing their meaning

The inspector uses `Effect.mapError` to translate a filesystem failure into its domain error.

packages/core/src/file-inspector.ts at 65e9465f38092e24486392f22c08f45d61230c20; lines 20-26; highlighted none.

```typescript
      const content = yield* fileSystem
        .readFile(path)
        .pipe(
          Effect.mapError(
            (error) => new FileStatsError({ path, reason: error.message })
          )
        );
```

Translation keeps the failed path and the source message. Callers receive `FileStatsError`, not a filesystem dependency.

If a domain error needs to carry an unknown source error, `Schema.Defect()` can describe that field.
Such a field does not itself turn an expected error into a runtime [defect](/lore/effect-basics).

## Recover or report at a named boundary

`Effect.catchTag` handles the selected failure tag. Other failures remain failed.
Use `catchTags` when several tagged failures need different handlers.

The CLI reports the inspection failure, then fails again:

apps/cli/src/cli.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 19-21; highlighted none.

```typescript
  Effect.catchTag("FileStatsError", (error) =>
    Console.error(error.message).pipe(Effect.andThen(Effect.fail(error)))
  ),
```

A fallback is appropriate only when its value is a valid domain result.
Do not turn a failed inspection into empty file statistics just to complete the command.

## Do not use orDie to hide ordinary failures

`Effect.orDie` removes expected failures from the typed channel by turning them into defects.
The inspection [machine](/lore/lifecycles-are-machines) uses it where the machine's result is handed back to Effect because its expected file failure already travels through the `Unreadable` outcome.
An unexpected actor failure or missing outcome is a programming failure at that boundary.

This is a specific boundary decision. File reads still return `FileStatsError` to ordinary callers.
Use `Effect.catchDefect` only where an integration boundary must inspect unexpected failures.
Do not treat it as general domain recovery.

## Common wrong approach

Catching every cause and returning success erases whether the program refused work or crashed.
A later caller cannot tell which repair is needed.
Keep refusal, unexpected failure, and successful completion distinct.

## Effect idiom and house rule

- Expected failures appear in the [Effect](/lore/effect-basics) type. Tagged handlers can recover without swallowing defects.
- In rat-stack, errors name their source and give repair guidance. Finite lifecycles use XState through the pinned Effect bridge.
- The application chooses which lifecycles need machines and which diagnostic fields each error needs.

See also: [schemas](/lore/schemas-define-the-boundary), [author-facing diagnostics](/lore/errors-are-part-of-the-interface), [independent failures](/lore/accumulate-independent-errors), and [lifecycles](/lore/lifecycles-are-machines). [Failures keep their meaning](/lore/failures-keep-their-meaning) maps failure kinds to retry, refusal, and escalation.

# /lore/errors-are-part-of-the-interface

Source: .brain/resources/lore/errors-are-part-of-the-interface.svx
SHA-256: 5ea983ef9a9c731d53ae37beb73281de0de292be2ae01e419328a1299d8c358c

# Errors are part of the interface

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

The [code-snippets design brief](/lore/code-snippets) requires an author-facing error for each rejected snippet.

Each error carries:

- A typed error tag: the name identifying the declared error type.
- The source document and line.
- The rejected request.
- Requested ranges and actual file length, when available.
- A repair instruction.

The `RangeOutOfBounds` error class also has a brand.
The brand stops two classes with the same fields from being assignable to each other.

Invalid metadata keeps its raw values. It has no decoded request yet.

The author needs the rejected input, its location, and a repair instruction. A stack trace alone cannot supply them.

Use the [error model](/lore/error-model) to separate expected failures from defects.
Use [schema decoding](/lore/schemas-define-the-boundary) to reject invalid input at the boundary.
Use [error accumulation](/lore/accumulate-independent-errors) to report unrelated failures together.

Related reading: *Exceptional Ruby* and *Confident Ruby*, both by [Avdi Grimm](https://avdi.codes/books/).

See the glossary for [diagnostic context](/glossary) and repair instruction.

## Sources

1. [Avdi Grimm's books](https://avdi.codes/books/)
   Avdi Grimm. Author and titles only; no claims about book contents. Accessed 2026-10-02.

   Effect contributors. Typed errors Accessed 2026-10-02.
