# Learn during real work

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Teach the technology and principles in play. Use the project as a worked example. Keep the current task moving.

## Start and stop

- Start only when the operator enables learn mode.
- When the operator turns learn mode on, act at once. Read `learnPreferences`, call `learnNext` with no arguments, and present the returned concept.
- If the tools are not ready, say in one line how to ask: "Say *next concept* any time, or keep working and I will explain ideas as they appear."
- Keep questions off unless the operator explicitly enables them.
- Stop tool calls and explanations when the operator turns learn mode off.
- Keep existing progress when stopping. Turning the mode off does not erase history.
- Record `dismissed` when the operator asks to stop presenting one concept.
- Do not promise a reset or signed-in sync. Those tools are not available.

## Use the local tools

The local tools need a rat-stack checkout whose CLI has the learn commands. Check before you build or pull:

```sh
git -C <checkout> status --porcelain
node <checkout>/apps/cli/dist/cli.js --help
```

- The help output must list `learnNext`, `learnRecord`, `learnPreferences`, and `learnSetPreferences`.
- Never pull, reset, or stash in a checkout with local changes. Clone a separate copy for the learn tools instead.
- Do not use the operator's working checkout when it is behind or dirty. A fresh clone keeps their work untouched.

Clone, then build the CLI:

```sh
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/joelhooks/rat-stack.git rat-stack-learn
cd rat-stack-learn
pnpm install
pnpm turbo run build --filter=@rat-stack/cli
```

Configure the agent's stdio MCP client to run this command from that checkout:

```sh
node apps/cli/dist/cli.js mcp
```

Add `--devtools` when checking recorded calls. The local tool descriptions say they use the local event log. Public MCP and HTTP progress tools use supplied progress and store no progress.

Feedback is a separate signed-in operation. It does not synchronize learning progress.

The default local store is `~/.rat-learn/`. `RAT_LEARN_DIRECTORY` selects another local directory. `RAT_LEARN_ORIGIN` selects the public deck origin.

## Display preferences

`~/.rat-learn/preferences.json` holds three display choices. It stays on the machine.

- **`width`**:
  - Values: `narrow`, `wide`
  - Default: `narrow`

- **`visual`**:
  - Values: `inline-text`, `rich`
  - Default: `inline-text`

- **`snippet`**:
  - Values: `full`, `terse`
  - Default: `full`

- Read it with `learnPreferences`. A missing file means the defaults.

- Change it with `learnSetPreferences` only when the operator asks.

- `narrow`: keep the snippet and diagram one after the other, as plain text in the reply.

- `wide`: the diagram may sit beside the snippet when the display allows it.

- `rich`: the agent's own display may render the diagram, but uses only the card's fields.

- `terse`: show the service declaration and the line that uses or provides it. `full`: show the whole snippet.

## Select and present

1. Read `learnDeck` and match public terms to the ideas in the work.
2. Keep that matching step local. Select only real concept ids from the deck.
3. Call local `learnNext` when an Effect, Alchemy, or XState idea appears in the work.
4. Set `context.ids` to those concept ids and `context.at` to the current Unix time in milliseconds.
5. You may use `context.terms` instead of ids. Pass only public terms from the deck.
6. The tool resolves a term's owner and offers an unmet prerequisite first.
7. Omit context to follow the ordered learning path. Dismissed prerequisites do not block it.
8. Set `context.asked` only when the operator asks for an explanation.
9. Omit `progress`. Omitted progress means none yet, and the local tools read their own log.
10. Follow the returned depth. Present one relevant concept at a time.

- **walkthrough**: Show the `plain` line first, then the claim. Show the card's `snippet` as a TypeScript fence and its `diagram` as a text fence. Link the page.
- **paragraph**: Give the source summary as a short paragraph. Link the page for more detail.
- **line**: Give one source-grounded sentence.
- **none**: Say nothing. The tool omits concepts that need no presentation.

Use the card's `snippet` and `diagram` exactly as served. The content build compiles every snippet against the pinned versions. Never write your own snippet or diagram for a card.

A card without a snippet uses its page's pinned excerpt and immutable revision. Never substitute current source for the pin. State when that card has no suitable excerpt.

Call local `learnRecord` only after presenting. Use a `shown` event with the concept id, actual depth, current timestamp, and version 1. Selection alone does not record a presentation.

## Record what happened

- Record `used` when the operator applies the idea in their own code.
- Agent-written code alone does not establish operator use.
- Record `got-it` or `skipped` only from the operator's words.
- Do not infer understanding from silence, elapsed time, or reading a page.
- Never send the observed code or the operator's words with the event.
- If recording fails, say that progress was not confirmed. Preserve the log and follow the typed error.

## Keep it quiet

- Never quiz unless the operator opts in to questions.
- With questions enabled, ask at most one short check-in per long session.
- Use a due concept for that check-in. Accept skipping it immediately.
- Do not ask permission again after the operator has enabled the mode.
- Stop check-ins when the operator disables questions.
- Do not introduce unrelated concepts to fill a learning quota.

## Without MCP

Read the public deck through either surface:

```sh
curl -fsS https://ratstack.sh/_content/learn.json
curl -fsS https://ratstack.sh/api/learnDeck \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' --data '{}'
```

Use the CLI commands for selection and recording. They use the same local store as stdio MCP. Read [the system check](/systems/learn) for a complete round-trip.

Build first, then run `node apps/cli/dist/cli.js learnNext`. Add a `--context` JSON flag for concepts in play. Record with `learnRecord --event`. Use current timestamps for real learning events.

If the deck or CLI is unavailable, report that limit and continue the task. Do not claim that progress was saved. Never hand-edit the JSONL files.

## Leave feedback with phone approval

Use this flow only when the operator asks to leave feedback on a public card. The server exposes these tools only when `AUTH_ENABLED` is true. If they are absent from MCP, report that feedback sign-in is unavailable on that surface. Do not retry.

1. Draft the feedback with the operator. Keep it about the public card.
2. Call `learnFeedbackStart` with an empty input.
3. Show the returned `userCode` and `verificationUrl` to the operator.
4. The operator opens the URL on their phone, signs in, and checks the code.
5. The operator chooses **Approve feedback only** or **Deny**.
6. Call `learnFeedbackPoll` with the returned `deviceCode`. Wait at least the returned `interval` between calls.
7. Stop on `denied` or `expired`. On `polled-too-fast`, wait the returned interval before another poll.
8. After `approved`, call `learnFeedback` with `token`, `cardId`, and the agreed `feedback` text.
9. Confirm storage only after the [capability](/systems/capabilities) returns a feedback id.

The credential permits `learnFeedback` only. It is not a sign-in session or a credential for another tool. It expires with the device grant. The provider's device-code lifetime is thirty minutes, and its polling interval is five seconds. A new device flow is required after expiry. Do not use the stock `/auth/device/token` endpoint; it is disabled.

Keep the credential out of local learning JSONL, feedback text, examples, and shared messages. Do not include private code, prompts, paths, credentials, or names in feedback. A failed call does not prove storage. Automatic retry can store a second feedback row; ask before repeating an uncertain write.

## Offer a skill in the session

Learn mode suggests skills. It never installs them.

1. When a card's route is `/skills/<name>`, or the work matches a skill, name the skill in one line and link `https://ratstack.sh/skills/<name>`.
2. Ask before loading it. Load only what the operator wants.
3. To load it, fetch `https://ratstack.sh/.well-known/agent-skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and follow it for the rest of this session.
4. Never run a skills installer. Never write a skill into a global, user or project skills folder.
5. If the operator wants a skill kept for good, they choose where it goes.

## Privacy

Keep progress local. Preferences stay local too.

Use the public endpoints for deck and card reads. Do not send progress to public selection or recording endpoints by default.

Requests contain concept ids, timestamps, depth, familiarity, and dismissal state only. Never include code, file paths, names, repository names, or prompts. The event log is authoritative. The CLI rebuilds `cards.jsonl` and `tasks.jsonl` from it.

## Lore on this page

- [MCP is another surface](/lore/mcp-is-another-surface)
- [The fence](/lore/the-fence)
- [One schema, three surfaces](/lore/one-schema-three-surfaces)

# /skills/learn-alchemy

# Learn Alchemy

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Alchemy 2 declares and deploys cloud resources through Effect programs. Effect describes work with typed failures and required dependencies. One program declares resources, bindings, deployment state, and the Worker that uses them.

A service is a named interface for one job. A Layer builds services and supplies their construction dependencies. A contract defines an action's name, input, output, failure, and metadata.

Start with this repo's Cloudflare resources. Alchemy also supports other providers. Learn the vocabulary to write infrastructure and check planned changes.

Sam Goodwin describes an Effect as a promise with more information: its return value, errors, and requirements. His Alchemy shorthand is "if it compiles, it should deploy and run." Use compilation for feedback. Check cloud API failures during deployment.

## The vocabulary

- **Alchemy Stack** groups one infrastructure program and its outputs. Rat-stack exports `Alchemy.Stack("RatStack", ...)` in `apps/infra/alchemy.run.ts`.
- **Provider** supplies the cloud API implementation. `Cloudflare.providers()` appears in the Stack options in `apps/infra/alchemy.run.ts`.
- **State** records the resources that a Stack already owns. Rat-stack keeps its own store, the Worker `alchemy-state-store-ratstack-state-store`, which both entrypoints load from `apps/infra/src/state-store.ts`. The excerpt below loads it with `ratstackState()`.
- **Resource** is a declared cloud object such as a Zone, DNS record, DNSSEC setting, or Worker. Each gets a stable logical name in `apps/infra/alchemy.run.ts`.
- **Binding** is a typed runtime value attached to a Worker. Rat-stack declares the `CODE_SANDBOX` WorkerLoader and four RateLimit bindings in `apps/site/src/worker.ts`.
- **Plan** shows differences between declared resources and stored deployment state before a provider changes anything. Read it with the `plan` script in `apps/infra/package.json`.
- **Stage** names an isolated deployment state. Rat-stack's production stage is `prod`; the unflagged default is `live_$USER`.
- **Profile** holds provider credentials for the Alchemy CLI. This repo uses an Alchemy profile, not environment variables, for Cloudflare authentication.
- **Adopt** means take ownership of an existing resource explicitly. The existing `ratstack.sh` Zone and its DNSSEC setting use `adopt(true)` in `apps/infra/alchemy.run.ts`.
- **Dev** is local workerd execution with `ALCHEMY_DEV=true`. Rat-stack uses it to skip the production Zone and DNS resources in `apps/infra/alchemy.run.ts`.

## Trace one deploy

Read `apps/infra/alchemy.run.ts` from top to bottom.

1. The file imports Alchemy, the Cloudflare provider, Effect, and the `Mischief` Worker from `apps/site/src/worker.ts`.
2. `Alchemy.Stack` creates the program. `Effect.gen` gives it a place to yield resources and return outputs.
3. `Cloudflare.providers()` and `Drizzle.providers()` supply provider operations. `ratstackState()` lets Alchemy compare this run with prior state.
4. `ALCHEMY_DEV` guards resources that should not be touched by local development.
5. The Zone is named `RatstackZone` and adopted because `ratstack.sh` already exists. A Zone normally retains on destroy, and this Stack does not opt into deleting it.
6. The DNS-AID SVCB and TXT records point agent discovery at the deployed site. They use the adopted Zone's `zoneId`.
7. `Cloudflare.DNS.Dnssec` keeps DNSSEC active. It is adopted for the same reason as the Zone.
8. `Mischief` declares the Worker with `ratstack.sh` as its custom domain, `www.ratstack.sh` as a redirect, and port 1337 for dev.
9. The Worker construction yields its WorkerLoader and four RateLimit bindings: `API_PER_IP`, `EXECUTE_GLOBAL`, `EXECUTE_PER_IP`, and `INTEREST_PER_IP`. `Effect.provide(Cloudflare.Workers.RateLimitBinding)` supplies the RateLimit client layer.
10. `apps/site/src/worker.ts` also yields the Interest and InterestIndex Durable Objects. `EVENTS_ENABLED` chooses `Basin` or `basinFoundation`: both keep the bucket, stream, and visitor salt; enabled adds the catalog, sink, and pipeline. The Worker supplies the subscriber delivery implementation when it starts, outside core.
11. The Stack yields `Website` from `apps/web/src/website.ts` and returns both `mischiefUrl` and `websiteUrl`.

The outputs omit the production DNS declarations:

apps/infra/alchemy.run.ts at 81a12c4b86cd65bf86e4bdba98eda122d0133844; lines 17-23,119-130; highlighted none.

```typescript
export default Alchemy.Stack(
  "RatStack",
  {
    providers: Layer.mergeAll(Cloudflare.providers(), Drizzle.providers()),
    state: ratstackState(),
  },
  Effect.gen(function* stack() {
    const website = yield* Website;

    const mischief = yield* Mischief;

    yield* mischief.bind`${website}`({
      bindings: [
        { name: "WEBSITE", service: website.workerName, type: "service" },
      ],
    });

    return { mischiefUrl: mischief.url, websiteUrl: website.url };
  }).pipe(
```

The Stack is an Effect. Importing it describes work. The CLI runs it during a plan or deploy.

### Follow the Worker bindings

`apps/site/src/worker.ts` exports `class Mischief extends Cloudflare.Worker<Mischief>()(...) {}` with `main: import.meta.url`, so Alchemy bundles the default Worker export. Its construction Effect yields bindings before it returns the `fetch` implementation. Alchemy populates `Cloudflare.WorkerEnvironment` dynamically; this repo keeps the expected binding shape in local types at that boundary.

apps/site/src/worker.ts at 81a12c4b86cd65bf86e4bdba98eda122d0133844; lines 109-122,178-184,381-383; highlighted none.

```typescript
      const stageRateLimits = rateLimitDeclarations(yield* Stage);
      yield* Cloudflare.RateLimit("API_PER_IP", stageRateLimits.API_PER_IP);
      yield* Cloudflare.RateLimit(
        "EXECUTE_GLOBAL",
        stageRateLimits.EXECUTE_GLOBAL
      );
      yield* Cloudflare.RateLimit(
        "EXECUTE_PER_IP",
        stageRateLimits.EXECUTE_PER_IP
      );
      yield* Cloudflare.RateLimit(
        "INTEREST_PER_IP",
        stageRateLimits.INTEREST_PER_IP
      );
    const environment = yield* Cloudflare.WorkerEnvironment;

    // SAFETY: these are the native runtime bindings declared above. Alchemy types the environment as a dictionary it fills in at runtime, so this is the one boundary cast.
    // oxlint-disable-next-line typescript/no-unsafe-type-assertion -- Alchemy types the Worker environment as a dictionary, so the declared bindings need one boundary cast.
    const bindings = environment as RateLimitBindings & {
      readonly CODE_SANDBOX: WorkerLoaderBinding;
    };
  if (globalThis.__ALCHEMY_RUNTIME__ !== true) {
    yield* Cloudflare.WorkerLoader("CODE_SANDBOX");
  }
```

`apps/site/src/rate-limits.ts` keeps the four native binding names and their numeric namespace IDs together. `rateLimitsFrom` calls the native `.limit({ key })` method and turns a failed runtime call into a defect instead of failing open.

`apps/site/src/sandbox-worker-loader.ts` consumes the `CODE_SANDBOX` binding. It loads a fresh Dynamic Worker with limits and `globalOutbound: null`, so the code-mode Worker can compute and call declared capabilities without reaching the network. A capability is one named action with shared value definitions and a server-side implementation.

Sam describes the constructor as a Layer: declare dependencies in the Effect, use them, then return the implementation. In his React analogy, dependencies are the hooks at the top. The returned Worker is the component.

Declarations and consumers share one construction Effect. The environment assertion relies on the declared bindings. Check missing bindings in the plan and at runtime; typecheck alone cannot prove they exist.

## Plan, then deploy

The scripts live in `apps/infra/package.json`:

```sh
pnpm infra:plan
pnpm infra:deploy
pnpm infra:dev
pnpm infra:destroy
```

Run the plan first. It shows `create`, `update`, `adopt`, and `noop` actions before a provider is changed. Review replacements, domains, DNS, bindings, and stage before approving a deploy.

Production is stage `prod`. Pass `--stage prod` to the Alchemy CLI. An unflagged deploy defaults to `live_$USER`, which can create a second Worker instead of updating production. Never run an indiscriminate stage destroy. Name the stage explicitly and read its plan first.

Alchemy v2 represents outputs as values whose contents become available during deployment. Resources can still reference one another. Sam compares this to Pulumi's output model. The engine sees the graph before it acts. The engine orders resource operations without hand-written await chains.

## Why not wrangler.toml or Terraform

Wrangler is a good Cloudflare-specific tool. This repo needs one Effect program that declares the Zone, DNS records, DNSSEC, Worker, and the bindings consumed by the Worker, so Alchemy is the chosen boundary.

Terraform would keep infrastructure and the Effect Worker in separate languages and graphs. Alchemy can infer the Worker binding wiring from the same construction code that consumes it, while still showing a plan first.

Keep an existing tool when it already owns the state and the team knows its review path. Choose Alchemy here because the typed application and the cloud graph are one lesson.

## Gotchas from this repo

- The Worker bundle uses Alchemy's Rolldown path, and Node's type stripping is outside the normal TypeScript program. A red `pnpm typecheck` does not stop Alchemy from producing a deploy plan or bundle. Run `pnpm turbo run check test build` first and inspect the failing task. Do not use a deploy to bypass a red gate.
- Cloudflare API changes have broken Alchemy releases before. Check the pinned version in `apps/infra/package.json` and the generated pins page before changing it.
- The repo pins Alchemy to a beta. Alpha and beta APIs drift. Read the current pins and vendored source before copying an example from elsewhere.
- Cloudflare rejected string rate-limit namespace IDs during a deploy even though the local type allowed them. `apps/site/src/rate-limits.ts` uses numeric IDs and documents the boundary.
- `adopt(true)` authorizes adoption. Without it, Alchemy refuses to take over an existing Zone. Keep adoption narrow and never assume a resource is safe to destroy.
- Profiles carry Cloudflare credentials. Do not add provider tokens to `.env`, source files, or Worker bindings for CLI convenience.

## Try it

1. Run `pnpm infra:plan` and read every action. Do not approve a deploy. Identify which resources are `noop` and which would change.
2. On a throwaway branch, add one temporary RateLimit binding in `apps/site/src/worker.ts`, consume it, and run the Worker typecheck. Remove it after seeing how the declaration and consumer stay aligned. Do not deploy it.
3. Run `pnpm infra:dev`. Alchemy starts the Worker in local workerd, using the `dev` port from `apps/site/src/worker.ts`; the `ALCHEMY_DEV` branch skips the production Zone and DNS resources.

# Learn the stack

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Start with `inspectFile`, a [capability](/systems/capabilities): one named action with a contract and a server-side handler. The [contract](/systems/capabilities) defines its name, input, output, failure, and metadata. The handler implements the action.

A service is a named interface for one job. A machine defines states and the events that permit movement between them. A [projection](/lore/one-capability-every-surface) builds a callable interface from capabilities.

Follow these parts, then try the hosted content tools.

Read [Effect basics](/lore/effect-basics) before this trace if the computation model is new. For implementation tasks, use [services](/lore/services-capture-dependencies), [Layer composition](/lore/layers-make-dependencies-explicit), and [testing](/lore/tests-that-earn-their-place).

## The pieces

- Effect describes work with typed failures and required dependencies.
- Schema defines accepted values and their runtime checks.
- A Layer builds services and supplies their construction dependencies.
- XState owns finite lifecycles. The Effect bridge runs their declared actors.
- TypeScript 7 and Effect diagnostics check types and Effect usage.
- Oxlint, Oxfmt, Vitest, and lefthook enforce [the fence](/lore/the-fence): checks and hooks that reject prohibited code and shortcuts.
- pnpm and Turborepo connect packages and cache checks.
- Alchemy declares the cloud. Follow [learn Alchemy](/skills/learn-alchemy) for the deployment graph.

## One action, five interfaces

```text
                     ┌─ CLI
                     ├─ HTTP
One Capability ──────┼─ MCP
                     ├─ code mode
                     └─ RPC
```

A [projection](/lore/one-capability-every-surface) exposes the same action through another interface. RPC serves browser clients. [Code mode](/lore/one-program-can-replace-several-tool-calls) lets agents compose calls in one program.

All five interfaces use one handler.

## Trace one action

The CLI uses `inspectFile`. The hosted site uses a separate content registry.

### 1. Define the contract

The [contract](/systems/capabilities) names the action and its input, output, and failure schemas.

packages/core/src/contracts.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 255-263; highlighted 255,258-263.

```typescript
export const inspectFileContract = defineContract("inspectFile", {
  annotations: { idempotent: true, readOnly: true },
  description: "Count bytes, characters, words, and lines in a file",
  failure: FileStatsError,
  input: Schema.Struct({
    path: Schema.String.annotate({ description: "File to inspect" }),
  }),
  output: FileStatsSchema,
});
```

`FileStatsError` belongs to the interface. The annotations mark a repeatable, read-only action.

### 2. Bind one handler

`implement` binds the contract to `runInspectMachine`. The registry includes the resulting [capability](/systems/capabilities).

packages/core/src/inspect-file.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 10-22; highlighted 10-12,14-15.

```typescript
export const inspectFile = implement(inspectFileContract, ({ path }) =>
  runInspectMachine(path)
);

export const capabilities = [
  inspectFile,
  ...flagCapabilities,
  joinInterest,
  listPrompts,
  getPrompt,
  listCafeNews,
  listCafeProjects,
] as const;
```

The handler starts a machine to read the file.

### 3. Put file work in a service

`FileInspector.make` captures the file system. Its `inspect` method reads bytes and maps file errors to `FileStatsError`.

packages/core/src/file-inspector.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 14-29; highlighted 15,20-24,28.

```typescript
  make: Effect.gen(function* makeFileInspector() {
    const fileSystem = yield* FileSystem.FileSystem;

    const inspect = Effect.fn("FileInspector.inspect")(function* inspect(
      path: string
    ) {
      const content = yield* fileSystem
        .readFile(path)
        .pipe(
          Effect.mapError(
            (error) => new FileStatsError({ path, reason: error.message })
          )
        );

      return summarizeBytes(path, content);
    });
```

The service exposes its [Layer](/lore/layer-constructor-pattern) beside the implementation. This follows [hexagonal architecture](/lore/hexagonal-architecture): composition supplies the file-system dependency.

packages/core/src/file-inspector.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 31-35; highlighted 34.

```typescript
    return { inspect } as const;
  }),
}) {
  static readonly layer = Layer.effect(this, this.make);
}
```

Callers ask the service to inspect a path. Composition chooses the file-system implementation.

### 4. Give the lifecycle named states

A declared `createEffectLogic` actor calls `FileInspector`.

packages/core/src/inspect-machine.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 26-30; highlighted 26,28.

```typescript
const readStats = createEffectLogic({
  effect: ({ input }) =>
    FileInspector.use((inspector) => inspector.inspect(input.path)),
  schemas: { input: Schema.Struct({ path: Schema.String }) },
});
```

The machine starts in `reading`. It finishes in `inspected` or `unreadable`.

packages/core/src/inspect-machine.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 40-64; highlighted 40,43,51,57,59,62.

```typescript
  initial: "reading",
  output: ({ context }) => context.outcome,
  states: {
    inspected: { type: "final" },
    reading: {
      invoke: {
        input: ({ context }) => ({ path: context.path }),
        onDone: {
          context: ({ event }) => ({
            outcome: inspectOutcome.Inspected({ stats: event.output }),
          }),
          target: "inspected",
        },
        onError: {
          context: ({ event }) => ({
            outcome: inspectOutcome.Unreadable({ error: event.error }),
          }),
          target: "unreadable",
        },
        src: "readStats",
      },
    },
    unreadable: { type: "final" },
  },
});
```

### 5. Project the registered actions

The command-line interface (CLI) projects capability lists for each server interface. HTTP uses stateless learning capabilities. MCP and code mode use their local learning counterparts. All three include `inspectFile`.

apps/cli/src/surfaces.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 25-33,40-51; highlighted 25-28,30-33,40,42,44,48.

```typescript
export const capabilities = [
  ...coreCapabilities,
  ...learnCapabilities,
] as const;

export const cliCapabilities = [
  ...coreCapabilities,
  ...localLearnCapabilities,
] as const;
export const http = toHttpApi("RatStack", capabilities);

export const tools = toToolkit(cliCapabilities);

export const codeMode = toCodeMode(cliCapabilities);

export const routes = Layer.merge(
  HttpApiBuilder.layer(http.api, { openapiPath: "/openapi.json" }).pipe(
    Layer.provide(http.layer)
  ),
  HttpApiScalar.layer(http.api, { path: "/docs" })
);
```

The RPC [projection](/lore/one-capability-every-surface) derives contracts from its supplied capabilities.

packages/capability/src/to-rpc.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 24-27; highlighted 24,27.

```typescript
export const toRpc = <const Caps extends readonly AnyCapability[]>(
  capabilities: Caps

  const contracts = capabilities.map((capability) => capability.contract);
```

A projection takes a registry and reuses its domain handlers.

### 6. Connect the CLI

`toCommand` derives each command. `inspectFile` also gets the `stats` alias.

apps/cli/src/command.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 22-35; highlighted 25-28.

```typescript
const capabilityCommands = commandCapabilities.map((capability) => {
  const command =
    capability === inspectFile
      ? toCommand(capability, {
          positional: ["path"],
          render: formatFileStats,
        }).pipe(Command.withAlias("stats"))
      : toCommand(
          capability,
          capability === setFlag ? { promptForApproval: true } : undefined

});
```

### 7. Compose the cloud

An Alchemy Stack groups one cloud infrastructure program and its outputs. Alchemy declares the Stack, Cloudflare providers, and state. The Stack includes `Mischief` and `Website`.

apps/infra/alchemy.run.ts at b4d6b8f499e57bc76914ad70df3a0c99751ae28c; lines 16-22,118-129; highlighted 16,19-20,118,120.

```typescript
export default Alchemy.Stack(
  "RatStack",
  {
    providers: Layer.mergeAll(Cloudflare.providers(), Drizzle.providers()),
    state: Cloudflare.state(),
  },
  Effect.gen(function* stack() {
    const website = yield* Website;

    const mischief = yield* Mischief;

    yield* mischief.bind`${website}`({
      bindings: [
        { name: "WEBSITE", service: website.workerName, type: "service" },
      ],
    });

    return { mischiefUrl: mischief.url, websiteUrl: website.url };
  }).pipe(
```

The Stack deploys the cloud applications. The Node file-inspection CLI runs separately.

## Try hosted search and read

Use [POST /api/execute](/llms.txt#run-code-one-program-instead-of-several-calls) for [code mode](/lore/one-program-can-replace-several-tool-calls). The [agent guide](/llms.txt) documents this search → read program:

```js
const found = await tools.search({ query: "cartridges", limit: 1 });
const page = await tools.read({ id: found.matches[0].id });
return { title: page.title, id: page.id };
```

Send it as a JSON `code` string:

```sh
curl --request POST 'https://ratstack.sh/api/execute' \
  --header 'content-type: application/json' \
  --data '{"code":"const found = await tools.search({ query: \"cartridges\", limit: 1 }); const page = await tools.read({ id: found.matches[0].id }); return { title: page.title, id: page.id };"}'
```

`read` takes the exact ID from `search`. This hosted program reads site content.

# /skills/model-a-protocol

Source: skills/model-a-protocol/SKILL.md
SHA-256: dda54becd77ad81c8827c1d2eeb8937d87fc599660745df8d38d0a5d33330913

---
name: model-a-protocol
description: Check a protocol with a small TLA+ model before you build or change it. Use when steps can interleave or die halfway, such as a crash between two writes, a retry after an unknown outcome, an alarm or sweep that redrives work, or two writers on one record. Also use when asked "can this race?", "what if it dies here?", or "model this", or before a durability design review.
plain: "Model the protocol in TLA+, break each guard in the model and in the code, and never count an unfinished check as a pass."
diagram: |-
  design note
    │
  spec + cfgs
    ├ safety ── exit 0, floor
    ├ liveness ── exit 0 or warn
    └ weaker ── exit 12, named
    │
  flip guard ── exit 12
  break code ── twin fails
    ▼
  review, then build
---

# Model a protocol

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

A protocol is a set of steps that share state, such as a request, a background delivery, a sweep and an erase on one record. Example tests run one order of those steps. A model checker runs every order within small bounds, including a crash between any two steps. It finds interleaving bugs that reading and example tests miss.

The worked example is the join-intake model in `packages/core/spec/`. Its `README.md` shows each part of this skill on real code. Its test is `packages/core/test/join-intake-spec.test.ts`.

## When to model

Model a protocol when its steps can interleave or stop halfway:

- A crash can land between two writes.
- A retry re-sends after an unknown outcome.
- An alarm, a cron sweep, or `waitUntil` finishes work the request started.
- Two writers can change one record.

Model it before the design review, so reviewers argue over a trace instead of prose. A pure fold, a read path, or a single atomic write does not need a model. Use a [property](/lore/property-based-testing) or a [model test](/lore/model-based-testing) for those.

A fix to a protocol that has no model does not wait for one. Land the fix with its failing-then-passing test.

## How to model

1. **Use the pinned checker.** `tla-ts` is exact-pinned in `packages/core/package.json` and is not vendored. The test runs its CLI as a child process, and you run the same binary by hand: `pnpm --filter @rat-stack/core exec tla-ts -config spec/<Name>.cfg spec/<Name>.tla`. Keep the spec to plain TLA+ that TLC also accepts.
2. **Make every await a step.** A crash can land between any two steps. Model the store's real atomicity. If one call writes a record and a second call writes its index, the model needs two steps for that.
3. **Write the assumptions down.** List each platform or provider behaviour the model relies on in the spec's `README.md`. Each one needs a test, or a weaker config that shows what happens without it.
4. **State each invariant in words.** Reviewers check the words against the formula. A protocol that owes work later (an alarm, a sweep) needs an invariant that the owed work stays findable, such as `OwedIsFindable`.
5. **Write the configs.** There are three kinds:
   - **safety:** `INVARIANTS`, small bounds. It must exit 0 and reach a minimum distinct-state count. A smaller count means the model stopped exploring.
   - **liveness:** `PROPERTY` only, under fairness and a finite crash budget. Every invariant also belongs to a safety config.
   - **weaker:** an environment the code does not rule out. The test expects exit 12 and the named invariant. The README records the harm and the backstop.
6. **Flip every guard.** For each invariant except `TypeOK`, replace one line of the spec so the guard is gone. Checked against only that invariant, the flipped spec must exit 12 and name it. Any other result means the flip tests nothing.
7. **Give each flip a twin.** A twin is a behaviour test that runs the real code through the same counterexample. Break the real guard once by hand, watch the twin fail, restore it, and record the date and failure in the README. The test checks that the twin's title and the code guard still exist. That check is a tie, not proof. Only a mutation proves the twin.
8. **Map actions to code.** The README's action map names the function and await behind each spec action.

## Read the exit code

The classifier in `packages/core/test/fixtures/protocol-spec.ts` covers every exit code:

| Exit                                                         | Meaning        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------- |
| 0, with a completed state count                              | pass           |
| 10 to 14 (assumption, deadlock, invariant, liveness, assert) | counterexample |
| anything else: 150, 151, 255, a signal, the budget kill      | not checked    |

**Not checked is never a pass.** On a safety config it fails the test. On a liveness config it prints a `::warning::not checked: <reason>` annotation and the suite continues; a counterexample still fails. Results hold at the stated bounds. Write "checked at these bounds", never "proved".

## What the fence checks

`join-intake-spec.test.ts` fails when:

- the safety config finds a counterexample, cannot finish, or explores fewer states than its floor;
- the liveness config finds a counterexample;
- a weaker config passes, or fails on an invariant other than the named one;
- a flip's guard is not in the spec exactly once, a twin title or code guard is gone, or the flipped spec does not fail its invariant alone;
- a malformed spec or a run stopped by its budget is reported as checked.

No rule forces a model onto every protocol yet. Reviewers ask for one when a change meets the conditions in "When to model".

## What it found

On its first run, the join-intake model found three ways to lose owed work or an erase marker. The Durable Object store writes a record and its sweep index in two calls. Its `setState` reads and writes in two calls. And an erase can land inside the request's commit. Each is a weaker config with its harm and backstop in the README.

Then it checked candidate fixes. Making the erase marker sticky passed the `JoinIntakeEraseSticky.cfg` invariants for late delivery writes, and that fix shipped with a twin. It does not settle `JoinIntakeEarlyErase.cfg`: an erase inside the request's commit can prevent the ready save while the uniform answer still leaves. The early-erase and sweep-index gaps remain open in `packages/core/spec/README.md`.

The obvious fix for the index was to mark it before saving the record. The model refused it in four steps:

1. The request saves the contact as `held` and dies.
2. The eraser marks the sweep index, ahead of its save.
3. The sweep reads the record, finds no marker, and clears the index entry.
4. The eraser writes the erase marker. The work is owed, and the sweep cannot find it.

The record and the index live in two Durable Objects, and no transaction spans them, so no ordering of the two calls holds the invariant. The fix that would hold keeps an outbox beside the record: the record, an index-owed entry with a sequence number, and an alarm are written in one transaction, and the invariant becomes "owed implies indexed, or the outbox is armed". That fix is still open, and `JoinIntakeMarkBeforeSave.cfg` records why the reorder was not enough. The reorder would have passed review, and the trace stopped it before it shipped.

Read [durability](/skills/durability) for the patterns these models check, and [add a lifecycle machine](/skills/add-a-lifecycle-machine) for the machines that run them.

## Lore on this page

- [Workers answer requests; Durable Objects own named state](/lore/workers-answer-requests-durable-objects-own-named-state)

# /skills/onboard-a-list

Source: skills/onboard-a-list/SKILL.md
SHA-256: 7cd2118eb2c179e503c381152089870d40abefa4180e1f84a639b3fc1ff1aab9

---
name: onboard-a-list
description: Analyze or migrate an email list. Measure sanitation rules, preserve stops, choose a cohort, and verify an authorized import or sending cutover.
plain: "Capture source facts, measure overlapping cuts, preserve stops, and verify the authorized outcome."
diagram: |-
  capture facts
        |
  measure cuts
        |
  choose cohort
        |
  approved writes
        |
  stops -> profiles
        |
  switch -> readback
---

# Onboard a list

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Produce a census, a versioned selection policy, and a private cohort manifest. Import or switch sending only within the task's authority.

For routine broadcasts to an onboarded audience, use the project's sending procedure.

This procedure defines a migration job. It does not install an importer.

## Start with the source and authority

Identify the source account, destination tenant, email topics, available credentials, and approved operations. Reuse an approved cohort choice. Ask only for missing decisions that affect the result or authorize a new live action.

Name the facts and their writer:

- The source owns contact, consent, stop, activity, and automation facts until cutover.
- `ReadListSnapshot` captures those facts through a job-shaped [port](/lore/hexagonal-architecture). Keep provider vocabulary inside [adapters](/lore/hexagonal-architecture).
- The pure planner derives counts, intersections, and cohort selection.
- Destination contact and stop services own imported state. Profile imports cannot lift stops.
- Policy and capture receipts identify the inputs. A private manifest records exact tenant-scoped recipients and matched rule ids.

Read [contracts and policy](https://github.com/joelhooks/rat-stack/blob/main/skills/onboard-a-list/references/contracts.md) when defining an [adapter](/lore/hexagonal-architecture) or import policy. Read [the count-only example](https://github.com/joelhooks/rat-stack/blob/main/skills/onboard-a-list/references/worked-example.md) when explaining overlaps.

## 1. Capture a read-only inventory

Inventory broadcasts, journeys, welcome flows, transactional/API callers, scheduled jobs, and historical link services. Measure actual sends over an explicit window. Enabled does not mean sending. A welcome flow may be the only active sender.

Capture every page of contacts, addresses, topic/channel/global preferences, and permanent stops. Include stopped addresses without profiles.

Reconcile unique keys, terminal cursors, export row totals, and available before/after counts. Record observation times and concurrent-change gaps. Claim a transactional snapshot only when the source provides one.

Keep recipient rows, signed URLs, credentials, and source cursors private. Reports contain aggregates and safe source receipts. Limit read credentials to the source account.

Use read-only export/search jobs only when the task authorizes them. They must not alter customer state.

## 2. Establish the stop floor

Separate authoritative unsubscribes, complaints, hard-bounce stops, and provider denials from delivery events and heuristics. A bounced delivery alone does not prove a permanent hard-bounce stop.

Resolve identity conservatively. Preserve stops without profiles and their original reasons. Never rewrite typo addresses or collapse plus tags. Use only documented identity normalization. Report ambiguity.

Before enabling destination sends, durably import and read back the complete stop floor. Profile imports and consent defaults must not lift it. Keep later source and legacy-link stops flowing until continuity is proven.

## 3. Measure each proposed rule

Decode policy data with [Effect](/lore/effect-basics) [Schema](/lore/schemas-define-the-boundary). [Pin](/skills/gardener) external lists by source, revision/date, and digest. Store thresholds, domain/local-part sets, windows, and actions in that policy.

Measure each rule against each original pool. Report independent matches, pairwise overlaps, exclusive matches, the union, and an ordered waterfall. Show newly removed and remaining counts. Never add independent counts.

Keep observations separate from person-level conclusions:

- Disposable-list membership supports a cohort-quarantine proposal. It does not identify a bot person.
- Query DNS once per distinct domain during research. Record resolver view, observation time, and failures. Empty MX can permit [address-record fallback](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321#section-5.1). [Explicit null MX](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7505) is different. Revalidate time-sensitive evidence before applying a cut.
- Role mailboxes, typo-like domains, digit runs, entropy, and creation bursts can match real readers. Keep them review-only unless the owner chooses a bounded cohort restriction.
- Search available positive login, purchase, and learning evidence before counting an activity-absence proxy. Missing history remains unknown.
- Distinguish human metrics, raw metrics, and first versus repeat timestamps. Security scans and privacy prefetch are not human engagement. Fast events do not prove bot people.

Do not invent missing evidence or measured precision. Label any analyst precision guess unvalidated. Keep it separate from measurements.

## 4. Choose and pin the cohort

Present alternatives and one recommendation. Explain exact counts, bounds, gaps, and tradeoffs.

When engagement is required, use positive human evidence. Explain which readers first-event-only history can miss. Do not substitute raw opens when human evidence is unavailable.

Let the owner choose unresolved engagement windows and optional restrictions. Pin source receipts, base manifest, policy digest, cohort digest, and destination tenant.

Dry-run and apply use the same pure planner and policy bytes. Changed policy or widened eligibility needs a new selection. Newly discovered stops always narrow it.

Read [verification properties](https://github.com/joelhooks/rat-stack/blob/main/skills/onboard-a-list/references/verification.md) before accepting the planner. Cover the deduplicated waterfall and the weak-signal boundary.

## 5. Dry-run and prepare the destination

Reuse owned destination contracts. When building automation, expose census, planning, and import as typed capabilities. Project CLI, HTTP, and agent tools from those contracts.

Dry-run exact identities, stop matches, ambiguous records, counts, and value-level readback. Use tenant-scoped [idempotency keys](/lore/http-responses-need-validation) and durable resume checkpoints.

For an authorized import, write stops first, then profiles. Do not discard rejected stop rows or mark partial work complete.

Prepare sender ownership, authentication, content, tenant-scoped routing, consent basis, unsubscribe handling, and historical-link continuity. Verify real bindings with authorized synthetic recipients. Preserve other mail systems on shared domains.

## 6. Make the authorized switch

For a hard switch, stop every old sending path. Prove that stop before enabling destination sends. Do not invent a parallel sending period.

Capture final contact, consent, and stop deltas through a recorded boundary. Describe and close consistency gaps before claiming completion.

Keep old unsubscribe/tracking links working when needed, with old sending disabled. Persist new stops before acknowledging them. Enforce stops at final dispatch. An eventually consistent cache alone cannot protect that boundary.

Enable only the approved cohort. Reconcile accepted, completed, failed, and unknown provider outcomes. Never blindly retry an uncertain send.

On harm, stop the affected destination path. Restart the old sender only when that recovery action is authorized.

Use a persisted lifecycle: capture → measure → choose → prepare → switch → verify. Put retries, deferrals, cancellation, and resume in XState. Run work through Effect actors under the project's pins. A delay proves neither failure nor completion.

## 7. Prove and report the result

Read back stops, exact profile values, cohort counts, and both dispatch controls. Prove a stopped synthetic address cannot regain eligibility through signup or profile import. Prove historical unsubscribe links durably stop later dispatch.

Verify topic behavior and tenant isolation. Use authorized delivery receipts for real-send claims.

After cutover, measure later eligibility from destination-owned human events. State which human events are recorded. A clock window passing does not justify widening the cohort.

Report analysis-ready, import-verified, and sending-verified separately. Include input digests, exact/bounded sections, overlaps, rejected records, checkpoints, gaps, and the next authorized move.

Keep raw manifests private. Scan shareable artifacts for recipient patterns.

Register an event watch for unfinished external work. Act when its result arrives. Reconciled receipts prove analysis. A report alone does not prove an import or send completed.

## Lore on this page

- [Bindings](/lore/bindings)

# /skills/profile-a-worker

Source: skills/profile-a-worker/SKILL.md
SHA-256: 5319707a033dd5ae0c8c01c39aed5fc5a96c868b1587569a5192ec6b794f87cf

---
name: profile-a-worker
description: Capture a CPU or heap profile of a deployed Cloudflare Worker or Durable Object and read it with pprof. Use when a Worker is slow, burns CPU, nears its memory limit, throws Exceeded Memory, or you need to know which function costs the most in production.
plain: "Send real traffic, capture a short profile of the live isolate, read the widest frames, and change one thing at a time."
diagram: |-
  traffic to the version
    │ during the capture
    ▼
  POST …/versions/<v>/profile
    │ cpu or heap, 1–50 s
    ▼
  pprof file
    │ go tool pprof -top
    ▼
  widest frames → one change
    │
  capture again, compare
---

# Profile a Worker

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Cloudflare can sample a deployed Worker or Durable Object while it serves traffic. The result is a pprof file. Each frame is a function. Wider frames cost more CPU time or allocate more memory.

Source: [Profiling in production](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/profiling-in-production/).

## Terms used here

- **Isolate:** one running copy of a Worker. A profile samples one isolate that is already loaded.
- **CPU profile:** where CPU time goes. It samples about every millisecond.
- **Heap profile:** where code allocates memory. It records a stack every 512 kB allocated. It does not show retained memory, so it cannot prove a leak by itself.
- **Flat:** cost in the function itself. **Cum:** cost in the function and everything it calls.

## 1. Pick the target

1. Find the deployed script name. Alchemy names it from the app, resource, stage, and a suffix. Read it from the Alchemy state or the dashboard; do not guess it.
2. Pick the version. `latest` is the newest uploaded version, which may not be deployed. After an upload without a deploy, use the deployed version's id.
3. For a Durable Object, use the Worker that owns the namespace, the namespace id, and the 64-character instance id.

## 2. Get read access

Use one of these:

- The `cf` CLI with its own login.
- An API token with **Workers Scripts Read**, taken from your secret store for this one run.

Profiling is read-only. Do not add the token to the repo, `.env.schema`, or CI. Deploy credentials stay in Alchemy profiles.

## 3. Send traffic during the capture

A capture does not invoke your code. It records only what runs during the window.

- Start a load loop against the routes you suspect, then start the capture.
- Keep the loop running for the whole duration.
- `No recent executions` or `no loaded isolate` means the version had no traffic. Send traffic, then retry.

## 4. Capture

API, 10 seconds of CPU:

```sh
curl --fail --silent --show-error --request POST \
  "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$ACCOUNT_ID/workers/workers/$SCRIPT/versions/latest/profile" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"duration_ms": 10000, "profile_type": "cpu"}' \
  --output worker-cpu.pprof
```

- `duration_ms` is 1000 to 50000. `profile_type` is `cpu` (default) or `heap`.
- For a Durable Object, add `namespace_id` and `actor_id` to the body.
- CLI: `cf workers versions profile latest --worker-id "$SCRIPT" --duration-ms 10000 --profile-type cpu > worker-cpu.pprof`.
- The dashboard has the same capture under the Worker's **Observability** tab, view **Flamegraph**.
- Captures are rate limited. On HTTP 429, wait for `Retry-After`.

Check the response before reading it. A failure returns JSON. A success returns protobuf.

```sh
file worker-cpu.pprof
```

The docs say the API returns gzip. In a capture taken on 2026-10-09, it returned raw protobuf (`application/vnd.google.protobuf`). pprof reads both.

## 5. Read it

```sh
go tool pprof -top -nodecount=25 worker-cpu.pprof
go tool pprof -top -lines -nodecount=15 worker-cpu.pprof
go tool pprof -peek 'functionName' worker-cpu.pprof
go tool pprof -http=:0 worker-cpu.pprof
```

- Start with `-top`. Ignore `(idle)` and `(program)`. Note `(garbage collector)`: a high share points to allocation, so take a heap profile next.
- Use `-peek` on a wide frame to see its callers and callees.
- Function names come from the bundle. If the bundler keeps names, they are readable. Locations point at bundle files and lines, such as `file:/bundle/worker.js:3348`, even when source maps upload. Search the bundle or the source for the function name.
- In an Effect program, the fiber runtime (`runLoop`, `makePrimitiveProto`, `succeedWith`) is the floor every request pays. Look below it for your own functions.

## 6. Act on one finding

1. Name the widest function you own and the route that reaches it.
2. Make one change. Common wins: compute a value once instead of per call, [cache a completed value](/lore/cache-completed-values), stop building objects you throw away, remove code that a flag only half disables.
3. Deploy, send the same traffic, capture again for the same duration, and compare the same frame.
4. Record the before and after numbers in the commit message.

One capture samples one isolate for seconds. Take two or three before calling a pattern. Say "this capture shows", not "the Worker always".

## Finish

- The profile file and the command that took it.
- The top frames you own, with flat and cum.
- One change and its measured effect, or the reason no change is worth it.

## Lore on this page

- [Workers answer requests; Durable Objects own named state](/lore/workers-answer-requests-durable-objects-own-named-state)

# /skills/query-design

Source: skills/query-design/SKILL.md

---
name: query-design
description: Design or review SQL reads, writes, scans, backfills, and slow database paths. Use before changing a store method or any loop that queries. Covers round-trip arithmetic, batching, keyset paging, index evidence, row budgets, PlanetScale Vitess limits, Hyperdrive connections, statement-count tests, and statement-template fences.
plain: "Count round trips first, bound each query, prove its index, and make tests catch extra statements."
diagram: |-
  question + caller + rate
    │ round-trip arithmetic
    ▼
  bounded store operations
    │ page parents
    │ batch children
    ▼
  EXPLAIN + count test
    │ manifest + plan fence
    ▼
  measured run + progress
terms:
  - "query design"
  - "round trip"
  - "keyset pagination"
  - "statement template"
prerequisites:
  - "/skills/add-a-store"
---

# Design queries around round trips

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

Count round trips before writing SQL. Small tables can still produce slow runs when each row needs several database calls.

```text
round trips per call × calls per run × RTT = wall time
```

RTT means round-trip time. This arithmetic estimates serial network time; query execution, decoding, and connection acquisition add costs.

Consider an illustrative scan of about 9k threads:

- Per-thread reads: 5 round trips × about 9.3k threads × 81 ms ≈ 63 minutes.
- Paged and batched reads: 2 round trips × 93 pages × about 100 ms ≈ 20 seconds.
- These are planning inputs. Measure RTT where the caller runs before choosing its budget.

A [capability](/systems/capabilities) call has a constant round-trip budget, independent of result size. State that number and bound its result. A scan costs O(pages), never O(rows). Count transaction control statements and any final empty-page probe too.

Done means the store implementation matches a written query plan, and checks detect violations of its statement and access-path budgets.

## 1. Name the question, caller, and rate

Record these before changing the store:

- **Question**: The fact or change the caller needs
- **Caller**: Capability, scan, export, or background job
- **Rate**: Calls per invocation and invocations per second or run
- **Authority**: System of record, derived copies, and writer
- **Row budget**: Maximum rows read with tables at 100× today's size
- **Statements**: Round trips per call, per page, and per run
- **Timing**: Measured RTT, predicted wall time, and observed page time
- **Concurrency**: Maximum simultaneous queries or transactions

Measure table sizes and inspect existing indexes. Keep credentials and row contents out of measurements and reports. Route operator, export, and monitor reads to a replica or a copy. Record any consistency tradeoff. Compare repeated joins or aggregates with a keyed [read model](/skills/add-a-store) before adding a hot-path scan.

## 2. Apply the shared rules

1. **Never query inside a loop over rows.** Page parents, fetch their children with one batched `IN`, then join in memory. Apply the same authorization filter to both queries. Keep analysis pure over the fetched rows. Bound child fan-out and result bytes too. Page children separately when one parent can exceed the batch budget.
2. **Use keyset paging, never OFFSET.** Order by an indexed tuple that ends in a unique column. Match the cursor predicate to each column's sort direction. Fetch `limit + 1` to detect another page. Emit a cursor from the last returned row. Exclude the extra probe row from the returned page.
3. **Name each query's index and prove it with EXPLAIN.** Use representative data and the actual query builder. Record the chosen `key`, access `type`, estimated `rows`, and sorting work for MySQL. Expect `const`, `eq_ref`, `ref`, `range`, or an index-ordered limit that meets the row budget. Equivalent plan fields apply to other engines. Inspect examined rows when the engine supports execution analysis. Fix full scans or filesorts on growing tables. Justify any index hint with plan evidence.
4. **Select only columns the caller uses.** Keep large bodies, JSON, and text fields out of counts and metadata scans.
5. **Keep transactions short.** Name the atomic writes or consistent reads that require one. Never wrap an entire scan in a transaction. Keep external I/O outside the transaction.
6. **State a concurrency bound.** Start production scans with serial pages over one connection. Measure before adding parallelism. Explain the load budget and why more concurrent work helps.
7. **Show progress on long runs.** Emit phase, completed pages, counts, and elapsed time to stderr. Use counts-only output. Set a measured stall deadline and return a typed failure with phase and completed count.
8. **Use a store boundary.** A [port](/lore/hexagonal-architecture) declares the operations that callers need. An [adapter](/lore/hexagonal-architecture) implements those operations for a provider. A [Layer](/lore/layers-make-dependencies-explicit) builds services and supplies their construction dependencies. Follow [add-a-store](/skills/add-a-store) for job-shaped operations and adapter Layers. Keep SQL, Drizzle, connection pools, and driver calls inside the adapter. Callers depend on the port.

A result limit bounds returned rows. EXPLAIN evidence must also prove the scanned-work budget. For tenant-scoped MySQL stores, lead the supporting index with the tenant key and preserve that filter throughout paging.

## 3. Check PlanetScale Vitess limits

These limits apply to PlanetScale Vitess transactional workloads. They do not describe PlanetScale Postgres. The [Vitess system limits page](https://planetscale.com/docs/vitess/troubleshooting/planetscale-system-limits) supplies the published values.

- **Transaction timeout**:
  - Published value: 20 s
  - Design consequence: Treat it as fixed in application configuration. Use short transactions.
- **Autocommit query timeout**:
  - Published value: 900 s
  - Design consequence: Page work well before the timeout.
- **Rows returned, updated, or deleted per query**:
  - Published value: 100k
  - Design consequence: Bound reads and bulk writes.
- **Result size per query**:
  - Published value: 64 MiB
  - Design consequence: Bound bytes as well as rows.
- **Transaction pool**:
  - Published value: Capped; capacity varies by instance type
  - Design consequence: Limit simultaneous transactions and keep them short.

The limits page says support can sometimes adjust limits per database. It offers no application setting for the transaction timeout. Do not make a design depend on a larger timeout.

Map a killed transaction to a typed adapter failure. Preserve the operation, provider code, and redacted cause. An error containing `1105` and `context deadline exceeded` needs timeout handling; `1105` alone is a generic error code. The [errors page](https://planetscale.com/docs/vitess/troubleshooting/errors) also documents `2013` deadline errors and `1105` transaction-aborted timeout errors.

Vitess pools MySQL connections through vttablet. `SHOW PROCESSLIST` shows those pool connections, rather than a one-to-one application-session list. Use application-side timing and provider query diagnostics to inspect a stalled run.

## 4. Keep Hyperdrive connections request-scoped

For the shared MySQL path, use mysql2 text-protocol `.query()` inside the adapter, as drovr does. Keep that protocol choice explicit in the query runner. Count every statement it sends.

Create the connection within the Worker request and reuse it for that request's statements. Release it through the request lifecycle. Hyperdrive owns reuse of underlying database connections across requests. Avoid a second pool or a module-global driver connection. See [Cloudflare's MySQL example](https://developers.cloudflare.com/hyperdrive/examples/connect-to-mysql/) for connection lifetime details.

## 5. Make checks stronger than prose

### Count statements through the real store

Use `it.effect` and a counting executor Layer at the adapter boundary. The executor port describes statement execution; its test wrapper counts calls while delegating to the real fixture executor. Keep counters scoped to each test. Exclude fixture setup from the measured call count. This is pseudocode for a consumer-owned port, rather than a shipped rat-stack MySQL API:

```text
it.effect("scan obeys its statement budget", Effect program):
  generate N parents and bounded children
  seed the native database fixture
  provide the real store with a counting executor Layer
  reset the statement counter after setup
  scan all pages through the store port
  verify complete results, ordering, and authorization filters
  assert statements <= planned statements per page × page count
                       + planned fixed overhead
```

Generate cases below, at, and above page boundaries. Include empty pages and parents with different child counts. Vary parent count within one page: its statement count must remain constant. Include cases where the planted N+1 exceeds the budget.

Replace the batched child read with one query per parent. The count test must fail. Restore batching and run it again. Record both outcomes before trusting the check. Check rows and bytes separately; a statement-count test cannot prove index use or bounded child fan-out.

### Commit statement templates and enforce a plan fence

A fence is an enforced check that rejects prohibited work. A handler is the server-side implementation of an action. A stronger check records every statement template the native suites issue, with its source site and exercising handler. Normalize placeholder-list lengths in `IN` and multi-row `VALUES`. Never record parameter values.

```text
committed manifest entry:
  template: normalized statement text
  sites: source locations that issue it
  handlers: named handlers that exercise it
  sentBy: Worker | operator | fixture | diagnostic

executor plan fence:
  normalize each application statement
  fail when its template is absent from the manifest
  fail when its source or execution surface is disallowed
  inspect each query's plan against its index and row budget

coverage check:
  fail when a required template has no exercising handler
  compare issued templates with each handler's declared templates
```

Count `begin`, `commit`, and `rollback`. Distinguish fixture setup from application statements. Capture driver or auth pools separately if they bypass the measured executor. Report uncovered paths as test gaps. Run the same real handlers natively and through a non-production Hyperdrive connection against a PlanetScale development branch. The native plan proves local access paths. The provider run proves protocol and decoding behavior on that route.

Plant a missing manifest entry and observe the fence fail. Restore it and record the passing coverage result. A manifest proves exercised statement coverage. Add fixtures for untested branches before claiming broader coverage.

## 6. Keep consumer details in their playbooks

- **drovr:** Uses Hyperdrive text-protocol `.query()`, a committed statement-template manifest, and a plan fence. Native MySQL 8.4 CI checks exercise its real store handlers. A provider runner checks the Hyperdrive route separately.
- **front-desk:** Uses Drizzle behind store ports. Scans from an operator computer page parents and batch child reads. Its playbook owns connection setup, scan phases, and progress counters.
- **AIH support:** Uses reader-role credentials for support reads. Its playbook owns allowed columns and authorization filters.

These examples describe consumer choices. A cartridge is a package for one job, with its implementation and required infrastructure. rat-stack's current database cartridge supplies D1 and Hyperdrive Postgres adapters. A consumer supplies its MySQL executor port and counting Layer through the same store boundary.

## 7. Read the prior art

[PlanetScale database-skills](https://github.com/planetscale/database-skills) is MIT-licensed. Read its material for deeper engine guidance:

- [mysql](https://github.com/planetscale/database-skills/blob/main/skills/mysql/SKILL.md) and [vitess](https://github.com/planetscale/database-skills/blob/main/skills/vitess/SKILL.md).
- [n-plus-one](https://github.com/planetscale/database-skills/blob/main/skills/mysql/references/n-plus-one.md) and [explain-analysis](https://github.com/planetscale/database-skills/blob/main/skills/mysql/references/explain-analysis.md).
- [composite-indexes](https://github.com/planetscale/database-skills/blob/main/skills/mysql/references/composite-indexes.md) and [covering-indexes](https://github.com/planetscale/database-skills/blob/main/skills/mysql/references/covering-indexes.md).
- [query-optimization-pitfalls](https://github.com/planetscale/database-skills/blob/main/skills/mysql/references/query-optimization-pitfalls.md) and [connection-management](https://github.com/planetscale/database-skills/blob/main/skills/mysql/references/connection-management.md).

Markus Winand's [No OFFSET](https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset), from *Use The Index, Luke*, explains keyset pagination. Measure real limits: count store calls as well as rows. Batching can move more rows without multiplying network round trips.

## 8. Finish with evidence

Report:

- Question, caller, rate, row budget, and concurrency bound.
- Each query, its named index, and pasted EXPLAIN evidence.
- Round trips per call and run, predicted wall time, and observed timing.
- Store port, adapter, statement-count results, and planted N+1 failure.
- Manifest coverage, plan fence result, and planted missing-template failure when that stronger check exists.
- Progress behavior, typed timeout handling, and untested provider paths.

Run the consumer's native checks and provider checks. In rat-stack, finish with `pnpm turbo run check test build`.

- [The fence](/lore/the-fence)
- [Cartridges](/lore/cartridges)

# Work in rat-stack mode

New on /news: [tla-ts 0.0.9 adds TLC's -continue](/news).

[AGENTS.md](/AGENTS.md) is law. [VISION.md](/VISION.md) sets the intent, reliability goals, scope, package-removal test, and shrinking debt. Use this skill to choose playbooks under those rules.

A capability is one named action with shared value definitions and a server-side implementation. A cartridge is a package for one job with its implementation and required infrastructure.

## Non-negotiables

- Start a todo list with reading the principles index below.
- Open every leaf that bears on a decision. Report which rules changed which choices.
- Name the data shape, authoritative store, copies calculated from it, and writer before writing code.
- Reuse stores when their facts and operation guarantees fit. Reporting does not justify gating unrelated execution.
- Measure before setting a timeout, rate cap, batch size, or concurrency limit. Put the baseline first; requested values remain hypotheses.

## Principles index

Leaves live in the repo; read them from a checkout.

**Product and UX**

- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/judge-through-the-person.md`: changing an interface or user-visible behavior.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/keep-boundary-words-honest.md`: naming failures, outcomes, and public claims.

**Architecture**

- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/one-contract-many-projections.md`: adding actions for agents or browser clients.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/keep-the-stack-floor.md`: choosing runtime patterns, infrastructure, and validation.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/prove-move-delete.md`: replacing an internal API or implementation.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/use-real-provider-guarantees.md`: choosing an adapter or testing its behavior.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/gates-guard-invariants.md`: adding a gate or approval check.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/keep-unknown-distinct.md`: handling crashes, refusal, or missing results.

**Data and truth**

- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/name-the-system-of-record.md`: adding stores, caches, aggregates, or nightly reports.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/store-source-facts.md`: capturing observations or interpreting missing fields.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/keep-execution-receipts.md`: recording runs or claiming an operation succeeded.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/scope-private-data.md`: handling identities, credentials, logs, or analytics.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/version-content-artifacts.md`: writing public content or quoting code.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/no-dual-writes.md`: copying a fact across stores or maintaining a read model.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/validate-before-durable-write.md`: recording rows, events, or snapshots.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/bound-every-read.md`: listing, querying, exporting, or rebuilding data.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/one-writer-per-partition.md`: updating shared mutable state.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/make-operations-idempotent.md`: replaying commands or recovering after crashes.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/subtract-before-you-add.md`: sequencing new work or removing unused interfaces.

**Durability**

- [durability](/skills/durability): any I/O boundary, pool, provider call, waiter, fan-out, flag, or gate. The hub lists seven patterns, each with its principle, example, and fence.

**Verification**

- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/check-the-actual-artifact.md`: finishing work or reviewing another agent's result.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/prove-the-recipient-path.md`: changing runtime wiring or deployed interfaces.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/tests-detect-broken-behavior.md`: adding tests or judging their coverage.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/find-the-cause-first.md`: fixing failures or slow runs.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/rebuild-what-you-run.md`: running or debugging an artifact someone else built.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/measure-real-limits.md`: setting budgets or diagnosing contention.

**Agents**

- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/look-it-up-first.md`: entering unfamiliar code or deciding whether to ask.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/ask-one-material-question.md`: reaching a decision that needs owner sign-off.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/own-your-wait.md`: waiting on CI, another agent, or a long local run.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/separate-writers-verify-readers.md`: dividing work or accepting delegated results.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/encode-lessons-in-structure.md`: correcting a repeated bad pattern.

**Prose and visual**

- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/use-plain-language.md`: writing docs, skills, or system pages.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/design-serves-function.md`: changing layout, focus, or visual emphasis.
- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/make-review-views-complete.md`: rendering evidence for people and agents.

**Cost and speed**

- `skills/rat-stack-mode/principles/optimise-the-whole-loop.md`: changing builds, tests, generation, or feedback time.

## Playbooks

Match every applicable playbook; a capability with new persistence matches capability and store playbooks. Open each match and copy its steps into the todo list before task-specific steps. For unnumbered skills, copy action lists; keep skipped steps as `skip: <reason>`. Finish with each matching playbook's report requirements.

- New action: [add-a-capability](/skills/add-a-capability).
- States, retries, or cancellation: [add-a-lifecycle-machine](/skills/add-a-lifecycle-machine).
- New persistence: [add-a-store](/skills/add-a-store).
- Existing email list or sending cutover: [onboard-a-list](/skills/onboard-a-list).
- Public prose or skill pages: [write-a-wiki-page](/skills/write-a-wiki-page).
- Security audit: [security-audit](/skills/security-audit), with the [rat-stack boundary map](https://github.com/joelhooks/rat-stack/blob/main/skills/security-audit/RAT-STACK.md).
- Package or interface choices: [keep-or-cut](/skills/keep-or-cut).
- Stateful design, replacement, or read-model design: [uncomplect](/skills/uncomplect).
- Pins, recurring bad patterns, or repository maintenance: [gardener](/skills/gardener).
- Peer research or shared dependency updates: [find-peers](/skills/find-peers).
- Cloud resources or unfamiliar deployment wiring: [learn-alchemy](/skills/learn-alchemy).
- Unfamiliar stack integration: [learn-rat-stack](/skills/learn-rat-stack).
- Crashes, flaky tests, wrong output, or slow runs: [investigate-a-failure](/skills/investigate-a-failure).

`write-a-query`, `add-a-read-model`, and `explore-limits` are planned. Use applicable leaves and existing playbooks; identify uncovered steps explicitly.

## Autonomy and child-project slots

Follow AGENTS.md's **Boundaries and sign-off** for autonomy. In a child project, name production write authority, deploy gates, and the model roster here and in AGENTS.md.

# /skills/security-audit

---
name: security-audit
description: Security guidance and vulnerability review for codebases, APIs, services, CLI tools, libraries, and daemons.
